#6748. Bill Hader Has Highbrow Taste in Children’s Movies

You can trust Bill Hader on movies. From gushing about John Ford and Akira Kurosawa in the Criterion Closet, to spoofing Errol Morris and D.A. Pennebaker in Documentary Now!, to creating, directing and starring in four seasons of HBO’s Barry—the SNL alum’s cinematic expertise is well-documented. Hader knows a thing or two about kids’ movies in particular, having lent his iconic voice to animated tentpoles like Inside Out and Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs. This week, you can hear Hader in The Cat in The Hat, a new adaptation of the 1957 Dr. Seuss classic, in which he voices the titular troublemaking feline.

Written and directed by Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja, this new iteration of the beloved children’s story is an inviting romp that is mischievous enough for kids, grounded enough for grown-ups, and teeming with gags and good nature that all can enjoy. The film is an ideal showcase for Hader’s gymnastic vocal talents, and also boasts Quinta Brunson, Matt Berry, and Giancarlo Esposito among its cast. (It’s a more family-friendly—though no less amusing—take on the Cat than when Hader last played the character, in a 2014 SNL sketch.)

A father to three daughters, Hader has seen it all—from Frozen and Tangled to Off Campus—and does his part, when possible, to pass down the classic films that were formative during his own childhood. “You don’t want to push it too hard,” he tells GQ on a recent call. “For every one I show them, there’s 10 that I start and they go, ‘Ugh, Dad, this is boring.’” The rest of us, however, are eager to take note. Below, Hader shares some of his favorite quote-unquote “kids’ movies” whose cinematic merit makes them a must-see at any age.

“When I was young, my dad told me that was a movie that he watched as a kid. I didn't grow up in a time when there were a lot of Westerns, but [for] my dad and uncles, that was all that was on TV.

What I was moved by was the relationship [between] Alan Ladd as Shane and this little boy [Brandon deWilde] enamored with a gunfighter. It has this heroic sensibility to it, but underneath was this honesty of, ‘You don't want that life,’ which I thought was interesting. To me, Van Heflin, the dad, was the cooler guy. So it upended those expectations of what the movie was going to be.

It has this ending where it's poignant and kind of sad, but I remember thinking, ‘Oh, that's good that that's what happens at the end of the story.’ It's a good coming-of-age story… It's kind of sneaky. You could see it on the face of it just being this cut-and-dry, Western-hero type of movie. But when you really think about it, even as a kid, I got a sense that there's a lot of depth to it.”

“Buster Keaton is one of my favorites, and that was one I showed my kids. I have three daughters. Now they're 17, 14, and 12, but at the time, they were very little. I'm a movie nerd, so I was gonna show them some silent movies, and I was like, ‘I know. Everybody's gonna roll their eyes at me for showing the kids silent movies. How pretentious.’ But they really responded to Buster Keaton, specifically Sherlock Jr. and Three Ages, his take on the movie Intolerance by D.W. Griffith. They just loved it, and it was fun getting to watch it through their eyes.

I recently took my youngest [to see] it at the Aero Theater in LA, and it still was great. To see a movie that was made over a hundred years ago still work on all [levels], like… it works better than most movies now. It's just very simple. [Keaton] wasn't some kind of auteur guy. He was a vaudeville comedian that was curious about filmmaking; what you could do with editing, what you could do with shots. And I think he ended up making the blueprint of how you shoot physical comedy and action. It’s pretty amazing.

What's interesting about some of those silent movies is that they don't really know what they're doing. The best stuff comes out of, ‘I don't know, I had this idea, let's figure it out in a really open, curious way.’ And in doing that, you invent the language.

Charlie Chaplin, too. [I’ve shown] them City Lights and The Circus and The Gold Rush. But they were really drawn to Buster Keaton, I think, because he was kind of dry and you didn't really know what he was thinking, and so you could put all your feelings onto him.”

“That's one that my parents showed me when I was a kid. It's a long movie, but it has so many crazy [moments] and a lot of physical comedy. I just love all those comedians in the movie. Every time someone pulls up, you're like, ‘Oh my God, it's Jonathan Winters. I love Phil Silvers. Oh my God, Spencer Tracy's in this movie!’ Dick Shawn is my personal favorite in that movie, the guy who's the real mama's boy.

It's kind of the one Stanley Kramer movie I like. Stanley Kramer movies tended to be, I don't know, a little sentimental, or overtly didactic or something, [but] this movie is just having a ton of fun. I have very fond memories of watching it with my parents and my grandparents. My dad was in town recently, and when I came home, he was watching it with my kids, and they were all laughing really hard and telling me scenes from it.

They really loved it, but [just like] with the silent movies, you don't want to push it too hard. For every [classic movie] I show them, there's 10 that I start and they go, ‘Ugh, Dad, this is boring,’ and I go, ‘Alright, we can watch Nobody Wants This or Off Campus.’”

“The Secret of NIMH was one that I loved as a kid, because it was ostensibly a kid's movie, but it was incredibly dark and disturbing. It has stuff that I still find really frightening. And I loved the mythology of it. As a kid, I liked the idea that in your backyard [there] could be this whole kingdom that you don't even know about.

There's specifically a shot in it with the crow, played by Dom DeLuise, and in the distance they see this cat. There's this long shot [of] this field, and then suddenly, just really quickly, you see this cat pop up and go back down under [as] it's trying to catch a bird or something. That shot had a huge effect on me. I thought, ‘Oh man, that's so terrifying.’

And then the story of the rats and NIMH, and they're all being tested on, and they fall into this abyss, and the whole ending where they're having this sword fight… I just thought it was fantastic. Everything was high stakes. And it wasn't Disney. I liked Disney, but Disney never went that dark.

Maybe not a lot of people agree with me, [but] I’m definitely someone [that] likes when something's scary for a kid, within reason. A lot of people are like, ‘No, no, no, they can't see that.’ And it's like, ‘No, let them see it. Get scared. That's good.’ I was happy that I was scared.

I'm sure if The Secret of NIMH came out now, they would have a whole room of executives going, ‘You can't have the owl with its head upside-down, turning around and with cobwebs all over him. It's just too scary.’ But for me, it scared me to death, and then I would keep watching it, and then it became less scary, and then I started to appreciate it. I think it's good for kids to be scared.”

“That movie came out when I was a freshman in high school. I got a job on the school paper, and my first job was to write a review of all the new movies, and it was the week that that movie came out. And so I remember I went with a notebook, I was writing my thoughts down, and then I ended up writing a pretty bad [review]. I liked [the movie] a lot, but my actual writing was terrible. The editors took it and rewrote it all.

But I loved it. I love Tim Burton. I loved the music in it, specifically the song that Catherine O'Hara sings as Sally; I think it's such a moving song. And Henry Selick’s direction in it is amazing. People always think Tim Burton made that movie. He didn't. It's Henry Selick. He spent every day there with those animators making that thing work.

I love the scope of it and how grand it is, from the beginning—that ‘This Is Halloween’ song, there's something almost operatic about it. And it's its own thing. The best stuff, to me, is always when the filmmakers and the writers [are] doing a thing that they want to see, and they trust an audience will get it.

When it came out, I remember it wasn't what it is now. It was kind of this weird oddity. And then as time went on… I remember moving to LA, and it was the 10-year anniversary of it, and they had a screening someplace, and I drove past all these people dressed like the characters, they had Jack Skellington t-shirts on and all that stuff, and I went, ‘Wow, that's crazy.’ Cause I was a huge fan of it, and had the soundtrack, and I absolutely adored that movie.

[Once] I had kids, it was one of the first movies I showed them, and they watched it every Halloween and every Christmas. My youngest daughter [recently] played Sally in a school play, and she got to sing that song, and so it was full circle. I got very emotional. I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, there she is, singing that song.’ And I had become friendly with Catherine O'Hara, and she passed away, and it was really… Yeah, I was a blubbering idiot when she started singing that song.”

#6746. Burberry Retail Sales Grow 4% in Q2, Carried by China and the US

Burberry’s comparable retail sales grew 4% on a constant currency basis in both the second quarter and first half of the fiscal year 2026/2027. For H1, Burberry’s group revenues grew 6% to €1.1 billion.

“Two years ago, we launched Burberry Forward [a plan to bring the brand back to where it was four years ago with a focus on outerwear and a diversified pricing structure]. Today, our brand is stronger, and our business is healthier,” said CEO Joshua Schulman on Thursday’s call. “We have delivered five consecutive quarters of growth and improved our quality of sales, which demonstrates that our strategy is working. This momentum stretches across product categories, channels, and geographies, and has translated into higher gross margin and increased profitability.”

Adjusted operating profit reached £62 million in H1, while gross margin rose to 68.3% — up 40 basis points from 67.9%.

Regionally, the Americas took the lion’s share of retail growth in Q2, up 11%, driven by local spending and activations, and healthy in-store conversion. Greater China followed, up 5% in Q2, a deceleration from Q1’s 9% climb. Burberry attributed this industry outperformance, in part, to the strong appeal of Burberry as a British heritage brand.

“We know that there’s been a lot of news about the challenging luxury market in China, but we’re being very deliberate, continuing to invest in our relationships with our customers in that part of the world,” said Schulman. “We understand that luxury customers around the world — particularly in China — are experiencing fatigue with exorbitant pricing, and in this context, our strategy of having enduring value and providing great value for money is resonating strongly with the Chinese customers.”

The Asia-Pacific region, excluding China, also grew in the quarter, up 3%, with South Korea growing 12%, driven by local demand. Japan was a weak point, down 1% in the quarter, attributed to softer tourism from mainland China. EMEIA also dropped 2%, due to softer tourism and traffic.

“It’s no secret that global tourism is down. So the local customer has been spending in their respective regions. We’re seeing globally that Middle Eastern, Chinese, European, and British customers are shopping at home,” said Schulman. “This is a trend we’ve been seeing all year long. There’s just less cross-border travel than there has been in the past.”

By category, womenswear led growth across retail and wholesale, growing 9%, followed by accessories (6%). Childrenswear and other also grew (5%), as well as menswear (3%).

The company didn’t share figures for outerwear, but reported double-digit retail growth in H1, led by the “rainwear” category. Lightweight gabardine designs and shorter styles performed through summer, while new cashmere and leather launches showed traction towards the end of Q2. Accessories also grew in Q2, and leather goods accelerated, boosted by strong performance in women’s handbags — particularly the vintage check and Cotswolds ranges.

Wholesale revenue grew 17% in H1. The company attributed this performance to the confidence of its partners, who are achieving high sell-throughs of Burberry products and continuing to invest in the brand’s designs. Licensing revenues dropped 5%. The brand opened seven stores and closed five, bringing the total to 412 directly operated stores as of September 2026.

The company also addressed its developing relationship with Frasers Group, which now has a 6% stake in the British brand. In October, Frasers Group had adjusted its stake in Burberry from 7.4%. This came after the growing retail group raised its position in the company from 6.3% earlier in the month, after upping it from 4.2% at the end of September. “We have a long-standing valued relationship with Frasers,” said Schulman. “They are an important wholesale customer for us in the United Kingdom, and now they are an investor. And just like we do with all of our investors, we will meet with Frasers Group in due course. In terms of their agenda, that would be a question for them.”

#6744. To Penny, or Not to Penny?

Few shoes are as essential in the modern menswear landscape as the classic leather loafer. Whether you’re dressing up or dressing down, it is the “the Swiss Army Knife of shoes,” an any-occasion solution to many footwear conundrums. But within the broader loafer genus, one particular species—the penny loafer—includes a divisive design feature: a small, coin-shaped slot in the leather strap “saddle” across the vamp of the shoe.

As the lore goes, Ivy Style pioneers and sock-hopping teens in the mid-20th century liked to store a penny in their shoes as “payphone change.” But now that payphones are a thing of the misty-eyed past and the American one-cent penny is no longer minted for circulation, is it still cool to put a penny (or any other coin, or coin-shaped object) in your penny loafers? What is the line between timeless and passé?

We invited two of GQ’s most well-heeled staffers, associate grooming and wellness editor Tyler Chin and senior style commerce writer Gerald Ortiz, to ponder the pros and cons of the penny loafer.

Mahershala Ali, an ostensible penny proponent, in London on October 19.

Tyler Chin, associate grooming and wellness editor: Sure! I’ve seen so many guys wearing loafers these days, and yet still haven’t seen any of them harking back to the shoe’s origins with a penny in them. Maybe I’m not looking hard enough or I’m not in circles where they are doing that, but it’s an inoffensive and easy way to accessorize the shoe. Plus, I had an English teacher in high school who did it, and while she wasn’t particularly cool, I did think the sartorial choice was neat.

Gerald Ortiz, senior style commerce writer: No. I feel like guys who put pennies in their loafers are either try-hards, or just learned about that particular piece of prep trivia. The only acceptable instance to wear a penny in your loafers is if you’re really about that prep/Ivy style, like Preppy Pete, or the guys who frequent Alfargo’s Market (shout out).

TC: I think the penny would be the most boring and obvious choice. If a quarter could fit in there, I think it’d be so funny if you were at a vending machine and short a few cents and settled up with the coin in your shoe. One time, the button on my pants fell off on the street and I lost it, but imagine I had a spare button in my shoe? I could reattach it right there and then! In the hypothetical I’d also need to be toting around a sewing kit, but hey, I’d love to think I could be MacGyver in that scenario.

GO: It doesn’t have to be anything at all. But if you’re going to do it, I don’t see why it couldn’t be another coin or object. It could be a Chuck E. Cheese token. Whatever you put in the slot, it would still be wack.

TC: I just got back from a trip to Tokyo, and I had a lot of leftover yen coins. Two of them—the five and 50 yen—have a hole on them, which differentiates them from your boring American coin. I’d throw one of them in my shoe and be one of those people who never stops talking about their travel abroad.

GO: I saw on Instagram someone stick a hundred dollar bill into their loafer and that was funny for a second. Then I scrolled on to the next meme.

TC: I’m pretty sure a coin that is that close to the ground will surely have a patina before the end of the day. Also, I can’t remember the last time I’ve seen a shiny new coin—who carries loose change these days anyway?!

GO: You know, it might be kind of cool to see a penny completely covered in verdigris slotted into your loafers. But maybe the coin should match the sheen of your loafers. I dunno, just don’t do it and you won’t have to think about it.

TC: Everyone I know is very familiar with my love of penny loafers. Lately I’ve been wearing them with bootcut jeans that are just a little longer than usual, so they have a nice drape over the shoe. Top-wise, I’d go with a tucked-in button up, T-shirt, or sweater. Pretty much anything that would go well with sneakers would be equally suited for wearing with loafers. Which is nearly all outfits.

GO: Penniless or not, a pair of wide khakis with a clean-to-slight break and a striped button-up is a failsafe outfit. It wouldn’t be very inventive, but it would pass muster for most conceivable situations. Vintage straight-leg jeans with good fades, a fucked-up band tee, and a sportcoat is also a great look. But the best looks are always the unexpected pairings.

TC: It’s sort of like how guys will go on and on about having functional sleeve buttons on a suit jacket. Is there any situation where you’ll actually need to unbutton those or do you just leave one or two undone to “stunt” on your unimpressed bros? If you really want to put a coin in your shoe for the sake of accessorizing your footwear, then by all means get a shoe with a functioning penny slot and use it! But if you’re doing it just so you can say “Yeah, these joints are the real deal!” and use it as an excuse to talk about the history of the shoe and why yours are superior, then I’d rather you wear lace-ups.

GO: I think it’s fine, even preferable to have a faux penny slot. It’s like how jeans still come with the watch pocket. It’s purely vestigial at this point, but would feel incomplete without it.

TC: One of these days, I’ll be telling my great-great grandchildren about the origins of the penny loafer and they’ll be confused because they would’ve never heard or seen the one-cent coin before. I’ll whip one out of my shoe and instead of being impressed they’ll chalk it up to another one of Old Man Ty’s tales from his youth, and tuck me back into the nursing home they checked me into.

GO: Lol. I guess it’ll make the penny more covetable. But it’ll be a long time before the penny becomes that desirable. That said, I love this British brand Six 95 that’s designing cool pieces using coins, so I can absolutely see more labels farming pennies for their clothes and accessories.

TC: Men will break up anything other than a toxic relationship. Loafers did nothing wrong and sometimes it’s just the person wearing them that needs to hit the curb.

GO: It makes sense. It’s like any trend, really. Even if they’re as versatile as we’ve been propping them up to be, loafers reached an inflection point where, for some guys, they’re just not the vibe anymore. But I don’t think they’ll dip so low to be thought of as cringe or as an emblem of the 2020s. They’re as classic as it gets and they’ll go through their own ebbs and flows.

TC: A quarter to increase my net worth 25-fold.

#6743. Friday the 13th Just Got a Little Luckier This Year

And you can thank Mercury Retrograde and Venus Retrograde finally coming to an end for that!

Friday the 13th may be tomorrow, but that doesn’t mean that luck isn’t in the air! This year on the longtime “unlucky” day, both Mercury Retrograde and Venus Retrograde (finally!) come to an end within a few hours of each other, bringing relief and clarity to your close relationships and ability to express yourself.

One retrograde is painful and frustrating enough, but over the past few weeks, you’ve navigated two at the same time, which can feel immobilizing at best and chaotic at worst. Fortunately, you’re reaching the finish line! Beyond the retrograde relief, Friday the 13th is actually considered an incredibly magical day, brimming with intuitive breakthroughs, despite its reputation.

For millennia, the number 13 was actually revered by many cultures and traditions all across the globe because of its connection to the average number of lunations we experience every year and also the average number of menstrual cycles a person experiences in a year. It was celebrated as a day to connect with and honor the Goddess. People who have periods are said to experience heightened intuition during their cycle and a strong connection to the other Realms. It’s through these associations that the number 13 carries deep and profound ties to magic, creation, manifestation, and birthing both new life and new desires and visions for your future.

Over centuries, the original meaning was distorted by patriarchal leaders and religions out of fear of collective feminine energy. By concocting false narratives and creating fearful myths about Friday the 13th, the patriarchal forces were able to exercise more control all while divorcing and dispelling many feminine people from reclaiming their own power and agency. Which is actually why many people consider this an “unlucky” day—but it’s really not at all! Once again, the patriarchy was out here ruining everything.

So clear your schedule because here come the divine downloads and revelations you’ve been waiting for. With Mercury Retrograde and Venus Retrograde ending, you’re ready to decide who and what from your past is worth clinging onto and which coffins you’re ready to put a final nail into. Here’s how this energy will manifest and how to make the most of it, based on your zodiac sign.

You’re done dealing with a lack of reciprocity in your connections. Whether it’s a current flame, ex, or BFF, it’s time for you to speak your truth and receive what you dole out so effortlessly to others. Your ability to be vulnerable and share your needs honestly can strengthen and deepen a connection in your life or protect you from someone who doesn’t deserve another ounce of your energy. There may also be a new contract or positive financial development on the horizon.

It’s time to prioritize your peace and set any necessary boundaries. Your daily commitments and responsibilities are just that—yours—and you can’t keep cleaning up other people’s messes. The end of the retrogrades ask you to confront close relationships in your life where you feel like your generosity is being taken advantage of. Standing up for yourself can bring more support and balance to your daily life as a result.

You deserve more joy in your daily life and you’re in a season of saying yes to whatever and whoever makes you happy. No one benefits from you staying so busy you can’t even hear your own thoughts in your head. The end of these retrogrades want you to reconnect with your inner child or inner teen who always made time for their creative hobbies, romantic connections, and had a zest for life—even on a Tuesday! You might experience a breakthrough in a romantic relationship or feel recommitted to a creative endeavor that fills your weeks with more passion and playfulness.

You’ve experienced healing in a close, private relationship. Maybe your sense of security in a relationship with a lover, family member, or roommate feels renewed and strengthened. You’ve reconnected with some of your own joy and found a lighter heart in the process that’s helped you understand and extend forgiveness to past situations and people that have caused hurt. You might also experience a creative renaissance, feeling inspired and confident enough to pursue who and what lights you up and that also offers security and grounding in your life, too.

You spoke your truth and are experiencing the ripple effects! Communication and self-expression are major themes for you as the retrograde ends, but especially in close relationships with chosen family, siblings, BFFs, and extended family members. There may be issues from the past that you’ve finally exposed, bringing relief, realizations and accountability in the process. Remaining silent to keep the peace benefits no one. There may also be a renewed sense of optimism in contracts or commitments that add to your sense of emotional or financial security.

You are practicing what you preach. There may have been moments in the past where your actions didn’t align with your personal values and, as a result, you felt tinges of imposter syndrome or shame. As the retrogrades end, you’ve reconnected with the power of your voice and aren’t willing to compromise what matters most to you so others can remain comfortable. Delayed contracts and negotiations also begin to pick up speed once again. You might also learn positive news that boosts your confidence or helps you invest in yourself or an idea you’re excited about.

This retrograde has been particularly trying for you and might have felt like a mini identity crisis. There’s no use in denying yourself pleasure any longer and you’re ready to debut a new, more authentic you to the world. You might also set new personal goals for yourself that feel like they shape your identity in some way—like pivoting and changing career directions or boldly addressing conflict and disagreements in a new way. You went through hell and back and you’ve finally reached your glow up—embrace it, take up space, and celebrate yourself along the way.

You’re more aware of who and what have been holding you back. As the retrogrades wrap up, you might understand some of your habits and patterns that have been self-fulfilling prophecies. You’ve engaged with your subconscious in a new way that’s helped you break certain patterns and kick limiting beliefs to the curb. You spent time with the emotions that drudge up past pain and grief. You spent many evenings crying on the bathroom floor. Now, you’ve done the inner work necessary to allow new growth and momentum to propel you toward the life of your dreams. A fresh start is around the corner.

You’re more aware of who is in your corner and who might not have your best interests at heart. The retrograde asked you to inspect and reflect on your friendships and sense of belonging. You took inventory of who you spend your time with and, not only how they made you feel, but also if your values align. Some friendships may wrap up while others are fortified. You may have also had a realization about your own self-defeating habits that are keeping you tethered to an old version of your life. You know what steps you need to take to reach your goals and dreams and the time to act is now.

You’ve felt directionless and the inability to act is so unfamiliar it felt overwhelming. The uncertainty about where you’re headed next is clearing and you can finally see the path forward. You might be ready to change career directions, accept a promotion, or finally start seeing yourself how others see you. There could have been certain people or friendships in your life that kept you in a cycle of seeking approval. But this retrograde helped you break free from living under other people’s expectations for your life and your joy. As you feel more centered and confident about who and what you want to prioritize in your life, you’re also ready to make meaningful progress on some of your longterm goals.

You felt unsure and maybe a little stuck, and you responded accordingly! There may have been a nudge or tug to go back to school, book travel to a place you’ve loved, or to hone a skill you used to enjoy. Picking up where you left off on a project and investing your mental energy in new (or old!) ways were just what you needed to feel inspired once again. There may also be certain conversations you’ve avoided with important figures in your life and, now, you feel ready to speak your truth. Your ability to speak about what’s been on your heart and mind will guide you toward the next step on your path—they are intrinsically interconnected.

You’re ready to invest in your future and take the next step. Maybe you’re ready to go back to school, sign up for a certification course, or write your memoir! You are more aware of how limited and precious your time and energy are, and how important it is to invest these precious resources into who and what makes you feel most alive. Vulnerable and healing conversations may also be a focus, asking you to navigate trust and intimacy in new ways that will either deepen bonds or ask you to move on in separate directions.

#6741. The Great Bear Rainforest: How Fashion Rallied to Stop the Deforestation of an Ancient Rainforest

This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa. Read more here.

The Great Bear Rainforest, spanning 6.4 million hectares from the Alaskan border to just above Vancouver Island, is the largest coastal temperate rainforest in the world, a critical carbon sink, and the only known home of the extremely rare white-furred spirit bear. Whales migrate through the rainforest year-round, and it is a major breeding ground for all five species of Pacific salmon. Thanks to the region’s heavy rainfall and nutrient-rich ecosystem, it also houses an array of ancient trees over a thousand years old, including sitka spruce (among the tallest trees in the world) and red western cedar (which hold deep cultural significance for the 26 local First Nations).

Until 2016, 90% of the Great Bear Rainforest was open for logging, and fashion was one of the industries profiting from it. The industry uses large quantities of man-made cellulosic fibers (MMCF) like viscose, modal and lyocell, which typically come from wood pulp. It also has a direct link to deforestation through wood-based packaging, and an indirect link through leather and cotton, which are often grown on deforested land.

Now, thanks to fashion brands joining anti-logging campaigners at a crucial moment, 85% of it is legally protected from deforestation and logging, the First Nations whose territories overlap with it are co-decision makers in its conservation, and there is a $120 million fund helping them transition to conservation-based economies. This is a rare example of fashion rallying around nature restoration and using its purchasing power for good, in partnership with other industries. Experts say it’s a blueprint the industry could apply elsewhere.

This “seismic” win took decades to achieve, says Nicole Rycroft, founder and executive director of non-profit Canopy, which works to conserve ancient and endangered forests around the world. While anti-logging efforts in the Great Bear Rainforest pre-date Canopy, the non-profit joined the campaign at a critical junction, leveraging fashion industry partners including H&M and Zara, to secure the groundbreaking land use agreement when momentum was slowing. “Canopy was one of several organizations that started working with international corporate customers of forest products coming out of that region to send a very clear signal that we don’t want to be sourcing from clear cuts of massive, ecologically critical, temperate rainforests, and we don’t want to be sourcing from spirit bear habitat,” she explains.

A decade on, Vogue Business invited Rycroft to reflect on what the Great Bear Rainforest can teach fashion about nature conservation, and using its purchasing power for good.

Logging happens at the beginning of the supply chain, several steps upstream from where brand traceability programs tend to stop. With such a complex, sprawling supply chain, and such a small number of brands on the hook to comply with traceability regulations, few brands have visibility beyond Tier 1 (garment manufacturing) or Tier 2 (fabric production). Logging would come under Tier 4. That’s why meaningful action starts with traceability, says Rycroft, so brands can understand where their deforestation risks are.

But brands don’t need a direct link to deforestation to make a difference in conservation campaigns. “Even if it’s not a direct or immediate sourcing link, the adjacency is really relevant,” says Rycroft. “Brands are still seen as important even if they’re not existing customers, because there is the potential for them to be future customers.”

Anti-logging efforts in the Great Bear Rainforest started in earnest in the mid-1990s, with conservation organizations standing shoulder to shoulder with local First Nations. But the forestry industry was powerful, so media coverage was largely limited to British Columbia, framing the conflict as a domestic “war in the woods” and failing to break through on the international stage. The turning point came when international brands began sending clear signals to the forestry industry that they did not want to source from ancient and endangered ecosystems. This included home improvement companies such as Home Depot and Lowe’s, as well as major retailers like Sainsbury’s.

But even after the various parties agreed to work toward a land use agreement, progress ebbed and flowed. It took more than a decade to reach a legal agreement, during which time brands and conservations continually applied pressure to keep negotiations on track. “It took consumer companies making phone calls and writing letters to individual forestry companies,” says Rycroft. Fashion joined in later. “The process was long and arduous, and for a long time, there was a blindspot around fashion’s footprint in the Great Bear Rainforest.”

It was Canopy that rallied the fashion industry to get involved. In 2013, it created Canopy Style, an initiative where leading fashion brands commit to end sourcing from ancient and endangered forests. One of the early adopters was Stella McCartney. Within a few months of signing onto the pledge, McCartney canceled her contract with a dissolving pulp mill on Vancouver Island, which was sourcing directly from the Great Bear Rainforest, Canopy discovered. “It sent a very clear signal that fashion is a force to be reckoned with,” says Rycroft.

Later down the line, around 2016, progress stalled again. The land use agreement was 18 months overdue, and even the most ardent supporters were starting to feel stuck. Canopy teamed up with national newspaper The Globe and Mail to host a customer-investor roundtable. The date was set for a month ahead. They invited leading politicians, the forest industry and the First Nations leaders that had been involved in the negotiating process, as well as conservation partners and 70 people representing 70 international brands, including Stella McCartney, Eileen Fisher, H&M, and Zara. “Within days of issuing the invitation, the spirit and intent at the negotiating table changed,” says Rycroft. Twenty-four hours before the roundtable was due to take place, the British Columbia government announced the draft land use agreement.

“Brands have incredible social capital and influence, in addition to being an important economic sector,” says Rycroft. “They can’t be afraid to lean in and flex that muscle.”

Brands that sign up to Canopy Style — or Canopy’s equivalent packaging initiative, Pack4Good — commit to stop sourcing from ancient and endangered forests. That’s the baseline, says Rycroft, the Great Bear Rainforest case study shows that fashion’s nature strategies need to go one step further. They also need to include scaling next-gen and circular alternatives that can ease the industry’s burden on nature, and the risk that burden poses to supply chain resilience.

“Next-gen and circular alternatives are the off-ramp from deforestation and forest degradation,” explains Rycroft. “Brands will not be able to eliminate — or even substantially mitigate — their risk of sourcing from high-carbon, high-biodiversity forests unless we have scaled alternatives.”

At last month’s Textile Exchange conference, Canopy walked the industry through Next Gen Warp Speed, its new initiative that makes the business case for brands to convert 5% of their MMCF basket to next-gen alternatives by 2028. Fashion’s struggle to scale next-gen materials has been well-documented, but Canopy is hoping that a 5% commitment is enough to tip the balance without putting a substantial burden on brands to fund the transition. “A big focus for us now is: how do we create the right conditions and pre-competitive vehicles to scale next-gen production?” says Rycroft.

Moving forward, Canopy is applying its learnings from the Great Bear Rainforest win to other critical ecosystems around the world. Top of its list are the Amazon rainforest and the Leuser Ecosystem in Indonesia, where it already has brand buy-in from the likes of Eileen Fisher and Stella McCartney. Rycroft says she is hopeful that fashion can make a significant difference in these landscapes, just as it did in British Columbia.

A few weeks ago, Rycroft traveled up to the Great Bear Rainforest to see the ecosystem Canopy had worked for so many years to protect. She sat on a riverbank and watched a spirit bear pick salmon out of the stream. “So many people dedicated their lives to this cause, or made a call at a critical juncture, to enable that to happen. It has made such a dramatic difference to the landscape. And now the Great Bear Rainforest truly is a landscape of hope.”

#6740. Meet the Cast and Characters of ‘The Good Daughter’

Excited to watch The Good Daughter on Peacock, but didn’t read the book by Karin Slaughter that it’s based on? Here’s everything you need to know about the cast and characters of The Good Daughter, without giving anything away. Well, maybe one thing. There’s a character who only shows up in one timeline for a reason. You might guess why, but I’m going to spoil it later just so we’re all on the same page.

First of all, no... this series is not connected to The Good Wife, The Good Fight, The Good Doctor, or The Good Place. As mentioned above, The Good Daughter is an adaptation of a bestselling novel that was published in 2017. The story is about two adult sisters who are reunited after a violent attack in their Georgia hometown brings up memories of the murder that tore them apart.

Slaughter herself adapted her book for the screen, penning the teleplays for all six episodes. Steph Green stepped in to direct and executive produce the series. As for the cast, here’s who you’ll see on The Good Daughter and who they play.

Sam, quintessential eldest daughter, left town and became a patent lawyer.

Rose Byrne’s breakout role in Hollywood was as a titular bridesmaid in Bridesmaids, though she had already appeared in films like Sunshine, Troy and Marie Antoinette at that time. That same year, 2011, she played Moira MacTaggert in X-Men: First Class and would reprise that role in a later film. She’s still best known for comedies, however, like Spy, Neighbors, and Neighbors 2 as well as horror movies like 28 Weeks Later and the Insidious films. Television-wise, Byrne played Gloria Steinem in Mrs. America and starred in both Physical and Platonic. She was nominated for an Academy Award for If I Had Legs I’d Kick You and a Tony Award for Fallen Angels.

Meanwhile, younger sister Charlie stayed in town and became a defense attorney.

Meghann Fahy was one of the breakout stars of The White Lotus’ second season, though she also hadn’t come out of nowhere. Prior to the HBO seires, Meghann made her Broadway debut in the Pulitzer Prize winning musical Next to Normal as an understudy and replacement for the character Natalie, then played Sutton on The Bold Type, and also acted in 83 episodes of One Life To Live. Since the HBO series, she has starred in the movie Drop and the Netflix series Sirens as well as The Perfect Couple and Your Monster. She is also a two time Emmy nominee, for both Sirens and The White Lotus.

Audrey Grace Marshall and Drew Cheek play Young Sam and Charlie

Flashbacks show who the sisters were before the trauma that shaped them.

Before The Good Daughter, Audrey Grace Marshall played Young Cassie on The Flight Attendent and was supposed to be in the Buffy the Vampire Slayer reboot. She did play Viv in the Fairly Oddparents live action reboot thing in 2022. Drew Cheek, on the other hand, has only one previous credit: a movie called F*ck Valentine’s Day.

Rusty is the sisters’ father and a former defense attorney with a reputation.

Brendan Gleeson is an Academy Award-nominated and Emmy Award-winning actor. He won the latter for playing Winston Churchill in the miniseries Into the Storm. You’ve seen him in the Harry Potter films, Braveheart, 28 Days Later, Gangs of New York, Troy, In Bruges, Edge of Tomorrow, Paddington 2, and The Banshees of Inisherin. Brendan has not done much television, but did lead Mr. Mercedes from 2017 to 2019, appear in the 2022 series State of the Union, and play Silvermane in Spider-Noir.

Lenore is Rusty’s secretary and the girls’ surrogate mother figure.

This is Harper Steele’s first ever professional acting credit. She is an Emmy winning comedy writer who worked at Saturday Night Live for 13 years and was a head writer for four of those years. Her other screenwriting credits include Eurovision Song Contest: The Story of Fire Saga and The Spoils of Babylon. Harper recently appeared with Will Ferrell in the road trip buddy documentary Will & Harper about their friendship before and after she came out as transgender.

Kelly is a suspect in a school shooting who Charlie chooses to represent.

Shayna Bernardo’s previous credits before The Good Daughter include the Lifetime movie Don’t Sweat The Small Stuff, an episode of Doom Patrol, and the horror movie Sorority Secrets.

Judith is an English teacher at a local middle school.

Paula Malcomson is probably best known for playing Katniss’ understandably checked-out mother Asterid Everdeen in The Hunger Games movies. She was also a series regular on the Battlestar Galactica prequel series Caprica, as well as Deadwood and Ray Donovan. She also recurred on Sons of Anarchy.

Huck is a teacher at the local middle school with a grudge against Rusty.

Jake McDorman is best known for leading roles in shows like Quintuplets, Greek, Manhattan Love Story, Limitless, Murphy Brown, The Right Stuff, Mrs. Davis and Dopesick. Olivia Williams plays Harriet ‘Gamma’ Quinn

First of all, no, this Harriet was the sisters’ mother and a genius physicist. Spoiler alert: she was violently murdered when Sam and Charlie were young girls.

You may know Olivia Williams from films like Rushmore, the 2003 Peter Pan, Anna Karenina, and An Education. Fun fact: Williams played Moira MacTaggert in X-Men: The Last Stand. Ben is Charlie’s estranged husband, and also a lawyer. So many lawyers!

Michael Dorman is an Australian actor with many starring roles on television to his name, including shows like Wonderland, For All Mankind, Patriot, Territory, and Joe Pickett. His film credits include Leigh Whannell’s The Invisible Man and Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales.

#6739. We’re in a James Bond Fever Dream Now

“Next James Bond ‘REVEALED,’” reads a headline published by The Sun last week. “After a loose-lipped co-star blabs secret after ‘a few lagers.’” The article suggests that Josh O’Connor, who has recently been named in the wider press as a last-minute hopeful in the race to find the next Bond actor, is the shoe-in to be 007—all based on what one of O’Connor’s cast mates in the theater production Golden Boy might have maybe told a stranger while drunk at The French House in London.

“They said that he had confided in them about getting the role when the cast of Golden Boy had celebratory drinks after the play finished its run on Halloween,” the article continues. So, there it is: we have our next Bond! Source: someone told someone else down the pub. No, really, honest!

This is nothing against O’Connor, mind. As Ben Allen argued in the latest edition of GQ’s Intermission newsletter, he would make for a killer, surprising pick, suggestive of an “actually new direction” delineating from the hyper-machismo that defined Bond through to the end of the Craig era. His characters tend to be quieter and more introspective; his performance style is similarly subtle. (The hipster choice? Maybe, but obviously a great one.) But the article is a symptom of how utterly insane the maelstrom of reports around the next Bond have become as we seemingly enter the casting endgame, with screen tests reportedly taking place in October. Further, producer Amy Pascal has said that we can probably expect an announcement to come before the end of the year.

Over the past weekend, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult emerged out of nowhere as having taken part in those aforementioned screen tests. Both would’ve come as whiplash to anyone who has had a passing interest in the endless Bond casting conversation: sure, they’ve been in and around the pack over the years, but given neither are called “Callum Turner” or “Jack Lowden,” the only speculated names taken seriously for much of 2026, they’re big—but both welcome!— shocks. I’m as much of an RPatz supremacist as anyone else who likes to think they know ball about films, the actor routinely being the best thing about his projects, from Nolan’s Tenet and all of his zany arthouse movies to both The Odyssey and Primetime this year. Much love to our man Hoult too, an underrated cornerstone of franchise cinema writ large, from X-Men to the new Superman. But still: what the hell?

In their own article about Pattinson and Hoult joining the race, Variety might’ve actually buried the most baffling lede: according to them, Harry Styles has “had discussions about the part,” while they also note that The Gentlemen’s Theo James—long thought out of the running—is actually yet to be ruled out. No shade on Styles, but he hasn’t been in a film since he briefly dipped a toe in acting in 2022’s Don’t Worry Darling and My Policeman, neither of which exactly kickstarted his movie career. And, like, he’s Harry Styles. Bond song? Yeah, we can see the vision. But the idea of him actually being 007 feels more like the product of an ayahuasca fever dream.

Regardless, Styles’s suitability for the role isn’t really the point. What’s more insane is that the Bond casting conversation only seems to have hit a level of psychosis as it nears the finish line: every other hour, the reported frontrunner switches from Lowden to Turner to O’Connor or Pattinson, a fever pitch of speculation and rumor-mongering that was tired before it was tired. Gary Oldman reckons it should be Lowden! Pierce Brosnan backs Turner! As one person astutely put it on Threads: “OH MY GOD JUST PICK A JAMES BOND. DO ANY JAMES BOND, JUST JAMES BOND A JAMES BOND.”

But it’s not just Bond himself, it seems. As I sat down to write this piece, an email hit my inbox from the publicist for a betting company. Subject line: “Maya Jama odds slashed to star in the next Bond film.” Damn it. Just bring back Pierce.

This article originally appeared in British GQ.

#6737. On the Podcast: Léa Seydoux Has a Shopping Problem. Plus: WNBA Star Gabby Williams!

More than a decade after winning the Palme d’Or for her role in 2013’s Blue Is the Warmest Color, Léa Seydoux—the self-proclaimed “queen of Cannes”—has confidently made the seaside city and festival her domain. Just earlier this year, she was there to celebrate two of her latest projects: Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster, which comes to Netflix on November 18, and Arthur Harari’s The Unknown.

For this Thursday’s episode of The Run-Through, Seydoux gathered with Chloe Malle and Taylor Antrim to discuss both ambitious films, which she shot shortly after giving birth to her second child.

“I used this body as a tool,” she explained. “Most of the time you see actresses with bodies that are very controlled, especially here in America. And if I can speak for myself, I’m a bit tired of seeing all these bodies that are just very skinny and not very real. I’m proud to show this body that we’re not used to seeing onscreen.”

The group also got into Seydoux’s long-time friendship with fellow French actress Adèle Exarchopoulos, who sported a “Léa Forever” T-shirt at Cannes this year. “We have a great relationship,” Seydoux said of her Blue Is the Warmest Color co-star. “I mean, we grew up together. She’s a great inspiration as well. I love her freedom—the way she’s not polished, you know? She is herself and very genuine.”

In addition to being a massively talented actress, Seydoux is also a “shopaholic,” as she puts it. She is a huge fan of buying vintage and scouring online auctions, though on this latest trip to New York, she made a stop at Los Angeles Apparel; they don’t have outposts in France. Art is another passion: “I collect paintings that represent motherhood.”

Also on today’s episode, Senior Wellness and Beauty Editor Margaux Anbouba and Global Talent Casting Director Ignacio Murrillo sit down for a chat with Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams about winning the WNBA championship last week.

#6736. These Cashmere Perfumes Are the Equivalent of Quiet Luxury in a Bottle

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Like wrapping yourself in a $400 cashmere sweater.

Not much compares to the snuggly feeling of a cashmere sweater against your skin, especially in cold weather. But if you don’t want to drop the $$$ on a whole cashmere wardrobe (if you do, make sure it’s Quince’s affordable cashmere), the next-best thing is a cashmere perfume.

Obviously, cashmere itself doesn’t have a smell. It’s a fabric, after all! But perfumers have found a way to capture that fluffy, cozy feeling through an accord called “cashmeran”—a blend of fragrance notes designed to evoke the soft, warm sensation of cashmere. Usually, that means it’s aldehydic (like fresh linens and cotton), warm, and a little bit powdery. But perfumes can still fall into the “cashmere” bucket even without a specific accord, usually using notes like creamy sandalwood and vanilla, warm amber and tonka bean, and even cloud-like musk and jasmine.

Smelling like cashmere has been my preferred way to embrace the homey feeling heading into winter. Nestling beside a fire, drinking a hot beverage, and wearing—you guessed it—a cashmere sweater has never been easier, so long as I have one of the below scents sprayed on. Keep reading for Cosmo editors’ top seven picks from brands like Byredo, Orebella, Phlur, and NOYZ.

"I always thought powdery perfumes would make me smell like a grandma, but either I'm inching toward grandma status or Angel Dust by Fugazzi is built different. It's powdery but not from heavy florals. Instead, the scent combines a mix of skin-like cashmere, musk, and amber. It's soft and reminiscent of the inside of a knitwear shop.”—BETH GILLETTE, BEAUTY EDITOR

“It’s hard to find a fragrance that straddles freshness and coziness, but this one does exactly that. Its moniker comes from a Brazilian Portuguese expression that describes the sensation of good vibes, happiness, and optimism, and it’s fair to say this perfume captures that sentiment perfectly. It oozes Brazilian warmth and sunniness and makes me want to book a trip to Rio.”—CELIA SHATZMAN, CONTRIBUTING WRITER

“I rely on body mists immediately after I get out of the shower to lightly fragrance my skin without feeling like too much. This one is my go-to right now (and the inspiration behind my current cashmere fragrance obsession). Even with nothing on (spicy!), my skin smells so toasty. It makes me want to immediately nuzzle into a plush robe.”—BG

“Unmute has a little bit of everything—juiciness from the plum note, spice from the cinnamon, musk from the amber, warmth from the sage, and sweetness from the pistachio—all wrapped in a cozy, comforting vanilla base. There’s something sexy and self-assured about the scent, without feeling too put-on or artificial.”—DANIELLE HARDMAN, CONTRIBUTING WRITER

“Milky perfumes are my favorite category of fragrance lately, and this does the lactonic, creamy fragrance so well. It’s not too sweet or cloying; instead, it leans on resinous amber, oak, and tonka bean to balance the scent. It’s like sitting by a fire, wrapped in the softest knits.”—BG

"I usually associate floral perfumes with spring and summer, but this one is undeniably perfect for cooler weather. Odéon is a smooth, rich rose scent, with a hefty dose of amber and cashmeran that gives it depth. It's inspired by Parisian cafe culture—and since I studied abroad there (hold the eyerolls), I feel qualified to say that this scent embodies the city’s romantic allure. It smells like window shopping in boutiques I can't afford and moonlit strolls along the Seine."—LAUREN GRUBER, COMMERCE EDITOR

“It’s an icon for a reason! Cashmere Mist is the OG of cashmere scents—it’s musky, powdery, and creamy, with soft woods and airy florals. My aunt was obsessed with this perfume in my youth, and I remember sneaking sprays of it whenever I wanted to feel like a ~sophisticated lady~”—BG

#6734. 5 Expert Habits to Find Inner Peace From Best-Selling Author Yung Pueblo

This is Expert Habits, a regular column in which thinkers, leaders, and other high performers talk about the habits and routines that help them live a better life.

Yung Pueblo wants to be clear on something: “I’m not a monk.” Sure, in his lifetime he’s meditated for over 13,000 hours, but he still enjoys the drama and chaos of Love Island UK like the rest of us. The best-selling author’s philosophical thoughts on self-awareness, emotional healing, and mindfulness have reached over 3.5 million followers since he first started posting to Instagram in 2013. His digital presence has since grown into published works of poetry and prose, including the New York Times bestsellers Inward, Clarity & Connection, and The Way Forward. Now Pueblo, whose real name is Diego Perez, is releasing a new book: Journey: The Year That Changes Everything (Penguin Random House), a 365-day guide to finding inner peace.

What exactly is inner peace to Perez? “It means that you have a good relationship with your emotions,” he says. “It’s that you’re able to feel your emotions without necessarily fueling the heavy ones.”

Inner peace, per Perez, isn’t a final destination. It’s about recognizing negative feelings and using tools you’ve learned to acknowledge that they’re happening without allowing them to take over your life. That’s what Journey—which debuts on November 10—is about. The following habits are just a few of the techniques he’s developed to do exactly that. Below, Perez explains the creative benefits of walking, the value of daily gratitude, and why you should protect your own peace even when others around you are chaotic—the latter of which makes keeping up with reality TV that much more enjoyable.

Yung Pueblo: “Oftentimes we have a relationship where we’re afraid of change and we need to realize that the universe that we live in, it’s totally founded on change at every level of existence—the atomic level, the biological level, the cosmological level. It’s because of change that we even have the opportunity to experience things. If our universe was static, we wouldn’t be having this conversation right now. So changing our relationship with impermanence and making it one where we actually get inspired to be more present. When we’re with our friends, with our family, with your mom, with your dad, you know that they’re not always going to be around. So the times when you are with them, to be ever more present, because you know change will happen at one point or another. Being able to have that presence just makes you have this ability to really enjoy some of the most beautiful parts of life.

“When it’s a sad moment, you have to be like, ‘OK, this is not going to last forever.’ But also in the precious moments, this isn’t going to last forever, so let me be here in the moment.

“Another way to look at it is that it’s defined by your relationship with change. So the more that you’re able to embrace change and flow with change, then your mind’s going to have less stress. But it’s probably one of the biggest challenges any human being can accept— willingly trying to change their relationship with change.”

“So much of our impulsiveness just comes from these lightning-quick reactions that we think are our nature. We think that they’re unchangeable, but the reality is that we can train ourselves to slow down to be able to ask: OK, is this me having an impulsive reaction right now? and then asking ourselves: Is this actually useful? Should I act this out or instead should I actually choose something that’s different than what I would’ve done in the past? And in the act of slowing down and being intentional, you just end up finding way better results. This is a real habit. You can learn that from meditating, you can learn that from therapy, but you can also just teach yourself the raw skill of feeling impulsiveness coming up and then challenging yourself to slow down.

“I’m not going to jump to conclusions. I’m not going to say anything right now. Let me just check in with how I feel, what actually feels true to me, and then put forward something that I think is actually going to be helpful as opposed to just something that I later regret.

“So if a friend of yours is telling you about something that they’re really mad about, they’re offering an invitation for you to be angry with them on their behalf. But instead I found that I don’t necessarily want to be angry, but I want to be able to hear my friends and offer support or a listening ear or whatever the situation is needed. At the same time, I can remain in my own energy while offering support to this individual. We get sucked into the energy of other people really, really quickly, but instead of getting sucked into someone’s chaos, for the past two years, what I’ve been working on is: Can I live in my peace and offer my peace as an invitation? They can join me in my peace too, if they want to, instead of me just getting sucked into their drama.”

“We fall into self-analysis when we don’t feel good. It’s just the worst time for you to be analyzing yourself about what you’ve done right, what you’ve done wrong. Negative self-talk isn’t productive. It’s good for you to be honest with yourself, but honesty also can come with gentleness and with self-acceptance. But when your mood is low, it’s going to be really hard for you to be gentle with yourself. So one thing I realize is when I don’t feel good or I’m over-exhausted from too much work or too much travel or whatnot, that’s the time for me to just suspend self-analysis and just treat myself gently—be mindful of what I’m saying to other people too, and just let it pass.

“And in the act of letting it pass, then you can do some more proper self-assessment because your best assessment is going to be when your mind is calm, not when it’s heavy.”

“Life is a long series of ups and downs, and there’s nothing wrong with that. But in the down moments, we tend to look at everything with such darkness that we forget that we still have access to clean water, that we still have access to food, that we have a house over our head. A lot of people in the world don’t have that. Having gratitude for the basics and the fundamentals really helps reset the balance where if something went wrong at work, you’re going to be okay, you’re going to be fine.”

“This is my recent favorite and it’s the newest habit that I picked up. You got to walk. You got to go for walks. Walking supports clarity, and I think it really supports creativity. I find that whenever I feel a little stuck with writing, just going on a 20- or 40-minute walk really helps to regenerate and create this new sense of clarity.”

#6733. Ariana Grande Brings Her Two Great Loves—Ricky Álvarez and Rare Vintage—to the Red Carpet

Ariana Grande brought two of her greatest loves to the red carpet last night: boyfriend Ricky Álvarez and a very, very good piece of vintage.

At the New York premiere of Focker-in-Law, the singer and actor made her first red carpet appearance with Álvarez since rekindling their romance earlier this year. And if their constant embraces, adoring glances, and kisses were anything to go by, the pair are very much still in the honeymoon phase.

Stylist Law Roach selected a vintage 1990s Badgley Mischka gown for the occasion. The delicate, spaghetti-strapped design featured a pale silver-gray windowpane check, a fitted bodice scattered with tiny beaded flowers, and a voluminous floor-skimming skirt. She accessorized with Swarovski Matrix hoop earrings—a recent favorite—and traded the flipped bob she’s been sporting of late for a sleek micro ponytail, tied with a little ivory ribbon. Makeup was also her go-to style of glowy and highlight-dominant.

Roach is on a particularly impressive archival streak of late. He’s been mining the fashion vaults for Kim Kardashian’s All's Fair press tour, pulling everything from 1990s Dolce & Gabbana to Paco Rabanne couture. Just last weekend, he dressed Anya Taylor-Joy in a spectacularly ruffled spring 1997 Pierre Cardin ensemble for the LACMA Art+Film Gala.

Grande has long been a devotee of fashion’s more whimsical, romantic history. Her love of vintage reached particularly fanciful heights during the Wicked press tours, but the singer has since held firmly to her soft, ultra-feminine aesthetic with 1950s silhouettes and diaphanous fabrics. At one point, her dedication to the look was so pronounced that some wondered whether she was quietly auditioning for a rumored Audrey Hepburn biopic. Roach revealed that he’d bought the Badgley Mischka gown months earlier, drawn to its connection with the era of the original Meet the Parents film.

Álvarez, for his part, kept things considerably more low-key. The dancer and photographer wore a relaxed black blazer over an open-neck white shirt, tucked into dark indigo jeans with rolled cuffs, a leather belt, and brown shoes. Some classic easy-going boyfriend dressing. He spent much of the evening with an arm around Grande’s waist, while she leaned into him, held his hands, and beamed up at him for the cameras.

Of course, the couple’s love story has its own history. Grande and Álvarez first met when he worked as a backup dancer on her Honeymoon Tour in 2015. They dated for around a year before splitting in 2016, and he later received a memorable name-check in her 2018 breakup anthem, “thank u, next.” Almost a decade later, however, things have come full circle. Rumors of a reunion began circulating this summer when the pair were spotted together in Austin, Texas, during Grande’s Eternal Sunshine tour, before more sightings followed in Florida and New York. By August, they were Instagram official, and Grande had debuted a new tattoo reading “I do love you”, seemingly matching a similar inscription on Álvarez’s collarbone. The two were also spotted arm-in-arm around London, where Grande completed her 10-night residency at the O2. She even began rewriting the Ricky lyrics in “thank u, next” onstage. At one Brooklyn show, she sang, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / We always find our way back.” By the tour’s September finale in London, the sentiment had become considerably more definitive: “I’m tryna make him my last.”

More recently, they’ve been enjoying some more ordinary couple activities, including cheering on runners at the New York City Marathon earlier this month. Grande has also enlisted Álvarez for a particularly kiss-heavy R.E.M. Beauty lip-product guessing game on Instagram. The adoration and affection is showing no signs of slowing down.

Between a decade-old romance finding new life and a beautiful dress pulled from the archives, Ariana Grande is making a persuasive case for revisiting the past.

#6730. Why This 251-Year-Old Watchmaker Is Suddenly Hotter Than Ever in 2026

Welcome to GQ’s 201-level Watch Glossary, breaking down the brands, advanced terms, and specific references that are essential knowledge for every serious collector.

Founded in the late 18th century by perhaps the world’s most famous watchmaker, Abraham Louis-Breguet, the eponymous brand was once the horologer to royalty. (He famously made a watch for Marie Antoinette that she unfortunately, ahem, never got the chance to wear.) Breguet is responsible for the tourbillon, an early self-winding mechanism, his famous namesake numerals that nearly every brand in Switzerland uses now, and much more. But despite its massive contributions to horology, the brand's pieces haven't caused frenzies among collectors like those from Rolex, Patek Philippe, or even Cartier. However, like Dune’s Bene Gesserit, the watchmaker’s plans are apparently measured in centuries. Recent signals point to the idea that Breguet may be entering a new golden era as collectors come around to its exquisitely made timepieces.

Follow the money, and you’ll quickly find evidence of Breguet’s glow-up. Late last month, at Monaco Legends Group’s fall watch auction, a 1970s-era piece previously owned by a 50-year veteran Breguet watchmaker sold for €221,000. That was nearly of the beginning of the brand's impressive run of auction that makes us wonder, What’s going on with Breguet these days?

Abraham Louis-Breguet isn’t the only hallowed watchmaker to steer the brand. Legendary names like George Daniels, F.P. Journe, and Michel Parmigiani have contributed to the brand’s legacy. At auction, many collectors are keying in on a period of Breguet led by Daniel Roth from the mid-’70s to 1987. After he left Breguet, Roth went on to found his own successful brand that now sells for six figures at auction. The combination of these two powers is proving irresistible to today’s collectors.

The Ref. 3050A was a signature piece of Roth’s reign at Breguet and epitomizes the designer’s contributions to the brand. Roth introduced the first modern piece from the manufacturer with a perpetual calendar. The piece’s guilloché dial is also a signature of the Roth era. The watch sold for €85,800 at the end of October.

The 3057 was the successor to Roth’s first watch at Breguet, the 3050. The big change is the transparent caseback. This lovely semi-skeletonized perpetual calendar hammered for some 200% above its estimate—not a huge surprise considering Breguet made only a couple of these a year when they were in production. Notably, thanks to the addition of that exhibition caseback, we can see the pretty, highly decorated automatic movement.

It’s platinum. It’s skeletonized. It’s got a tourbillon. It’s got a matching bracelet. It’s accompanied by all its factory goodies. What else could one ask for in a pre-owned Breguet? Still, a $387,000 hammer price is a remarkable outcome.

Classique Grandes Complications ref. 5447

This oversized perpetual-calendar minute repeater, likewise executed in platinum, commanded almost $271,000 at Phillips this weekend—proof positive of the appeal of classical Breguet looks mixed with modern movement technology and finishing.

An evolution of the Daniel Roth-era ref. 3350, this gorgeous tourbillon wristwatch features one of the hallmarks of Breguet’s signature style: a beautifully guilloché dial combined with blued steel hands and a Roman-numeral minute track.

Breguet took a significant left turn in the 1950s when it began producing the Type XX flyback chronograph for French military aviators. It still serves as an important pillar in the brand’s lineup today.

Introduced in the late 1980s, the ref. 3350 is Breguet’s first wrist-worn tourbillon—a significant milestone for the brand that invented the complication. Emblematic of the Daniel Roth era of Breguet production, it has since become a neo-vintage classic.

Released in 2025 in celebration of the firm’s 250th birthday, the Classique Souscription uses a single hand to tell the time against a Grand Feu enamel dial mirroring vintage Breguet pocket watches. Just this week, the maison followed it up with the platinum version seen above.

The Expérimentale 1 is the first step in a new collection of envelope-pushing, ultra-complicated watches. Fitted with advanced materials, the “1” features watchmaking’s very first high-frequency tourbillon, which beats at an astounding 10 Hz. This is a great way forward for modern Breguet—a model that embraces the brand’s tradition as the industry's most inventive watchmaker.

Now a quarter-millennium old, Breguet has one of the most extensive histories of any watchmaker still in operation, with records reaching back generations. Its finishing is exceptional; its complications are rooted in some of the earliest experiments by one of the world’s most famous horologists; and its designs are superb. As prices continue to skyrocket for watches at auction, especially for hotshot newcomers, it’s exciting to see one of the most storied brands in history catch fire, too.

#6729. Kim Kardashian Plays Nurse in One of Louis Vuitton’s Rarest Runway Looks

Kim Kardashian has been raiding the fashion archives with extraordinary enthusiasm of late, but her latest vintage pull comes with a health warning. Enter: a very rare, almost 20-year-old Louis Vuitton nurse uniform, complete with a monogrammed lace face mask, personalized cap, and coordinating accessories. The look, from Marc Jacobs’s spring 2008 collection for the house, is a heart-palpitating piece of runway history.

The ensemble was sourced by stylist Law Roach from the personal archive of Lauren Pyes, a Boston-based Harvard University employee and avid collector of Jacobs-era Louis Vuitton, whose extraordinary collection Vogue first explored last year. Pyes has spent years scouring resale platforms, boutiques, and obscure corners of the internet for some of the designer’s most coveted creations, amassing what she affectionately calls the “Marchive.”

“Law reached out to me a few months ago and was interested in pieces of the Marchive," Pyes tells Vogue. “Suffice to say, I was thrilled to loan them to him.” When Roach first contacted her, she could scarcely believe it was him. “I kept toggling back and forth to make sure it wasn’t a spam account!” she recalls. “Although he has a larger-than-life public persona, Law is deeply kind and gracious in addition to being the visionary he is rightly lauded as. I have so much respect for his dedication to telling stories through fashion and his commitment to finding the pieces that do exactly that.”

And few collections have quite as much storytelling potential as Louis Vuitton’s spring 2008 offering. Presented in Paris in October 2007, the show opened with a procession of supermodels—including Naomi Campbell, Stephanie Seymour, Eva Herzigova, and Nadja Auermann—dressed as nurses in sheer, pastel-colored uniforms, black lace masks, and white caps. The inspiration was the American artist Richard Prince, whose provocative Nurse Paintings informed the collection and accompanying collaboration with the house. Reviewing the collection at the time, Vogue’s Sarah Mower described it as a “typical Jacobs coup of multidimensional, referential, and self-referential significance,” and a “hilariously kinky parade” that “reflected Jacobs’s way of walking the line between creative freedom and commercial innovation.” It was one of Jacobs’s most deviant, deliciously strange runway spectacles.

The shoes from Louis Vuitton spring 2028.

The full look, as sourced by Lauren Pyes.

Kim Kardashian’s interpretation was remarkably faithful to the original. She wore the sheer, short-sleeved white nurse’s coat cinched at the waist over a delicate, peach-colored silk dress, with white stockings and peep-toe heels. A black lace Louis Vuitton face mask covered her mouth, while a white nurse’s cap (commissioned by Roach and reimagined by legendary milliner Stephen Jones) bearing a red “K” sat atop her sleek dark hair. In her arms was another treasure from the collection: an Aquarelle Papillon bag. The shoes also hailed from spring 2008.

Bringing together such a complete ensemble was no small undertaking. “I sourced these pieces from all over—including platforms like Poshmark and Vestiaire Collective—for over a year,” Pyes explains. The dresses have become a particular obsession: she has owned four, including a pink silk satin version that remains in her permanent collection. Vogue actually purchased another of the orange dresses—the same color Kardashian wore—from Pyes a little over a year ago. But the real rarity is the mask and overcoat, which Pyes considers among her most treasured finds. Earlier this year, the ensemble was exhibited at the Savannah College of Art and Design (SCAD), where it even caught the attention of one of its original creators.

“I had it exhibited at SCAD back in April, and Stephen Jones—who made it in collaboration with Louis Vuitton—was apparently surprised that it even existed!” Pyes says of the mask. “If the person who made it was in disbelief by seeing it, I guess that means it is pretty rare!”

Kardashian and Roach have been on a formidable archival streak throughout the All’s Fair press tour, resurrecting everything from ’90s Paco Rabanne couture to vintage Dolce & Gabbana and Jean Paul Gaultier-era Hermès. The Louis Vuitton nurse look is their most playful fashion deep dive yet.

And for Pyes, it’s precisely that irreverence that makes the Jacobs years so compelling. She points to the extraordinary creative team behind the collection, including Peter Copping, then head of womenswear and now creative director of Lanvin, and Camille Miceli, currently at the helm of Pucci. “This collection and these pieces are so special because they highlight what Marc and his team did so well—seamlessly integrating fashion and art into a cohesive and powerful narrative,” she says. She remembers the supermodel casting, the nurse uniforms, and even Jacobs taking his final bow beside a custom Vuitton trunk playing an episode of SpongeBob SquarePants. “There are so many elements that were unexpected and genuine in a pre-social media age.”

Pyes, of course, has continued to do some killer sourcing. She’s recently completed a “trifecta of accessories” from the Louis Vuitton fall 2011 collection, better known as the “Fetish Collection.” This includes a shearling porter hat, mask hair accessory, and a patent leather bib. On the non-vintage side of things? “I am champing at the bit to receive the custom order I put in from Marc’s Spring 2027 collection,” she shares. “After more than 40 years, he continues to create incredible fashion and I feel fortunate to be adding this ensemble to the Marchive!”

Whether Kim’s look was a Halloween latergram, another cheeky press tour outing, or just a moment of play inside an impressive archive, for now, is anyone’s guess. Whatever the occasion, Pyes is delighted to see the collection enjoying a new life in the public imagination. Nearly two decades after its debut, Jacobs’s peculiar, provocative vision remains as potent as ever. “These clothes are not just beautiful and special,” she says, “but also consequential. This collection walked almost 20 years ago and yet continues to figure so largely in pop culture and the imagination of fashion lovers.” Nurse Kardashia, the defibrillator please!

#6728. Meghan Markle Confirms a Burgundy Coat Is a Stylish Alternative to Navy

Head-to-toe burgundy is the look of the day.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry recently took part in their first official engagement since returning to British soil, and to mark the occasion, the Duchess of Sussex wore an all-burgundy ensemble.

The pair arrived in Nottingham last month to visit a youth and community charity, when they were pictured greeting fans outside. Meghan opted for a high-waisted slimline midi skirt, paired with a brown-toned roll neck and a single-breasted oversize coat in a matching hue. She finished the outfit off with simple court shoes.

Sitting somewhere between cherry and oxblood, burgundy takes its name from the red wines of France’s Burgundy region (what’s not to love?). It’s luxurious without being loud, and, crucially, is very easy to style. Even those of us who rarely stray from head-to-toe black can dabble in the shade without feeling out of our depth.

The color has infiltrated every corner of fall wardrobes in recent seasons, from standout leather and liquid satin to plush knitwear. Across the fall/winter 2026 runways, designers made the strongest case for burgundy with slews of the shade seen across Elie Saab, Max Mara, and Julien Dossena. Elsewhere, Balenciaga proved that the wine-tinged hue can perform just as well as any neutral, opening the show with all-black looks before quickly introducing the moody hue.

Meghan is not the only notable person to be favoring burgundy right now. Just this week, Victoria Beckham stepped out in a burgundy midi skirt, while the Princess of Wales also leaned into the trend with her handbag of choice.

If Meghan’s outfit shows us anything, it’s that the rich hue is an excellent alternative to black or navy this season, and should be worn as such. Below, our picks of six alternatives to introduce into your rotation once the temperature begins to properly drop:
