#6727. Why Blake Griffin Couldn’t Leave Basketball Alone

Twelve years ago, I was sitting in Blake Griffin’s house, listening to him tell me that under no circumstances would he stay around basketball after he retired. “Well, look who’s a liar,” he says now.

Griffin is a former NBA All-Star who played for 14 years, many of them for the Clippers, before announcing his retirement in 2024. He now has his own show, The Stepback with Blake Griffin, and a weekly gig with NBA on Prime, as part of their studio show. “I always thought that there was a little bit too much negativity when it came to scrutinizing players,” Griffin says. “This is a job that 400-something guys have. It’s extremely hard. I don’t need to go on TV and I don’t need to tell everybody that the guy that went three for 17 sucks at basketball. He doesn’t.”

On The Stepback, Griffin puts on a suit, sits behind a desk, and addresses a big, sports-related topic each week: the media, taxpayer-financed stadiums, the rocketing costs of youth sports, and so on. Like him, the show is unexpectedly funny, frequently insightful, and a good hang. In this conversation, he and I discuss the Clippers then and now, retiring at 34, and what it was like to have some rude journalist visit his house, all those years ago.

The following conversation is lightly edited and condensed from the latest episode of One More Question with Zach Baron. Watch below or on YouTube. Listen on Spotify or Apple Podcasts.

Blake Griffin: It’s funny, being 37 now, looking back at that time, and being like: “Man, I didn’t know what I was doing.” I can’t believe people were entrusting me with having a house and a car and doing all these adult things. I wasn’t an adult yet.

Well, in fairness to me, I’d only been living there for four years—no, I think it was fairly new at the time. I moved into that house at the end of 2013 and we spoke the next year. So over time you collect more stuff, figure out your taste.

He walked me through the entire party for—it felt like an hour, I don’t know, I had lost track of time. When you’re holding a 70-something-year-old man’s hand who’s not related to you, being introduced to party guests—and I think I was 19 at the time, I’d just gotten drafted—time sort of slows down. So I don’t know how long it was. Could have been half a day. But yeah, from the first time I met him, it was a very different experience.

Everybody, when I first moved there, was like, “Where are you from?” I’m like, “From Oklahoma.” And they’re like, “Oh, so—horses?” I’m like, “Well, yeah, but also cars.” It’s a civilized place. Culture shock in just that—I didn’t live in Hollywood, but you’re just in LA and that’s the epicenter of so much. It was a lot, but also you’re so focused when you’re 19. Apartment, practice facility, airport—those are the three things that I did. So it kind of gave me time to grow up. And then when we met, I was a much more seasoned man at 24, 25. It’s crazy looking back, because you’re like, “Man, I can’t believe I moved there at 19.” I tell people all the time, I grew up in LA.

I didn’t really dwell on that question. I don’t know. It was cool. I really enjoyed our conversation.

No, it’s fine. I was going there on my own. It’s fine. I’m happy to give one. I did. I enjoyed our conversation. I was actually thinking about it on the way here. Those are the best conversations—when you can just sit and talk and there’s not just these six questions that you’ve got to hit. You just let the conversation go where it goes. That’s what the conversation felt like to me.

Well, look who’s a liar. You know what’s crazy is, I never envisioned myself doing the NBA on Prime Show. And even until I retired and had conversations about going to join TNT or ESPN, whatever it was, and I still didn’t want to. And it really was Amazon getting a part of the TV rights and them really wanting to do a show differently than what was already on air. And that intrigued me because I thought there was this space in the NBA particularly where you can just analyze games, you can talk about basketball. And I always thought that there was a little bit too much negativity when it came to scrutinizing players. This is a job that 400 something guys have. It’s extremely hard. I don’t need to go on TV and I don’t need to tell everybody that the guy that went three for 17 sucks at basketball. He doesn’t. He had an off night. Instead, maybe I can walk you through some of the things he maybe could have done differently or some of the things he did well and it just wasn’t his night.

It’s kind of how I talk just in real life. I don’t want to harp on somebody who’s going through a shooting slump. Trust me, no one in the world wants to shoot better than the guy who’s in a shooting slump. It happened to me. Trust me. So I don’t need to come on TV and talk about it. So it’s kind of the same way I talk to people just in real life about certain games or what happened with this, what happened with that? It doesn’t always have to be negative.

I still do. I think that the day that I am bitter, or the day that I watch the game and I only see it from a negative standpoint or I’m like, “Back in our day, we didn’t do this or these guys are getting paid too much money”—I think that’s probably the day that I don’t need to do this anymore, because if I’m not going to adapt to where the game is today, I think that’s where you end up being jaded and you end up being biased in your observation or your analysis. And that’s what we’re hired to do, give our analysis. But it’s also like: Give your analysis on basketball today. It doesn’t matter what happened back then. And so my biggest thing too is every year I try to spend time with coaches, GMs, whoever it is, to keep understanding where the game is going, because it does change. Basketball evolves and you have to evolve your mindset around it.

We’re actually boys now. We went and did this golf thing together. I can’t lie. I was always just like, “What? Why? Give me a break, man.” I never was like, “Gosh, Charles is awesome.” Then you spend time with him and you see who he is and I appreciate it. I wasn’t the only person and at times it’s also not unwarranted. There’s games I played bad, I could have done better and this and that. And if that’s his style and that’s how he does it, that’s totally fine. It’s not that you can’t be critical. I just think I wanted to do [it] a little different.

There are definitely guys like that. My advice, if you’re in that spot, or something I wish somebody had told me when I was in this transition of really trying to develop my game, but also I was known for being aggressive, athletic, attack the rim, is you can continue to develop this skill and you continue to work on your game, but don’t go away from the things that got you to this place in the first place. So I would say to guys, use your athleticism, get to the rim, put pressure on the rim and then let that be your play making because now people have to rotate over, they have to help. Now you can open up different parts of your game. So a lot of times players hear all this like, “He can’t do this, he can’t do that.” And sometimes you kind of block out what you do well and you’re just so focused on what people are saying you can’t do.

Yeah. I mean, it’s almost impossible not to. I wouldn’t read tweets. I don’t read mentions during the season especially, but I wouldn’t put a lot of thought into comments, but it’s hard not to... When you’re just watching sports and you love watching sports and there’s morning shows on and it’s all around you, you’re going to hear stuff. And then there’s also the side of you that you know what you need to get better at as well.

I watched the game a little bit differently. I think as a player, I was watching so much of player tendencies, like I’m going to be guarding this guy in a couple days, or whatever it is. You’re also watching plays, you’re seeing teams run different sets. And now I’m interested a little bit more in the chess match that’s happening because trying to analyze, you’re looking at, okay, “What are the matchups? What would I have maybe done differently in that matchup? What could they do differently? What worked well? What didn’t work well?” And then you’re watching both sides of the ball, obviously. So it’s a lot of the same obviously basketball viewing, but I think when you’re trying to watch from an analyst perspective, you have to be a little bit more all-encompassing. When I’m watching as a player at night, if we don’t have a game, I’m not really tuning into, “Oh, since so-and-so got a tech, they’ve been on a 7-0 run,” but that’s something you clock now because it’s part of telling the story of the game.

I think it was my time. I think when I got to the point where I still enjoyed the game of basketball, but I was enjoying less and less everything else that came with it. My last several years I was in Detroit, I was in Brooklyn, I was in Boston, and my kids are in school in Los Angeles. So being away from them was tough. Even getting to see them once a month is still a little bit brutal. Or you’re on the road, you come back here, you get a couple days. So that wore on me. I also had an unfortunate amount of injuries, and I felt like I was having to put just as much in just to practice and then recover from that practice and then get ready for the game the next day, and it became this whole thing. I felt like I wanted to walk away from basketball on my own terms. I had a chance to go play another year and took some time to think about it, and I just felt like it was my time.

I don’t think there was a specific moment. I did remember when training camp came back around that next season and I was still trying to decide and I realized I didn’t feel like I was missing anything. I was like, “Oh, all right. Not as scary as I thought it would be.” Then as the season went on, I just didn’t see myself going back. I remember I was playing golf with JJ Redick once before I retired. This was before he took the job with the Lakers, and he said something to me that just stuck with me. He was like, “I’m telling you, you won’t be truly happy until you retire.” It kind of shocked me. Because he and I played together for five years, I think, and we were so similar in the way we prepared and the way we worked and how much we cared about the game that it just is this all-encompassing, obsessive thing. And it’s hard to really appreciate the little things, and it’s hard to appreciate making your own schedule. The school drop-offs, first day of school, doing all these different things. That’s sort of the way I took it, and the way I think that he meant it—is it’s such a grind, mental grind, physical grind, of putting literally everything you have into this thing. And then when you’re done, you just find this new sense of peace.

It’s amazing. I mean, I hope that they understood why I was having to be gone so much, but just being present is such a huge, huge gift. I mean, literally yesterday, my son had a football game that was two hours outside of LA. I drove two hours to watch an hour and a half football game, and then two hours back, and I was so happy. Now their games are what brings me sports joy.

It’s definitely scary because it’s also the one thing that you’ve done your whole life. And you also have to think—I dropped out of college. A lot of guys don’t even go, or guys are maybe there one year, and you don’t get the college experience of the workload and classes and graduating, internships, your first foray into the working world and you’re learning all these lessons and figuring out who you’re going to be, who you want to be, or how to operate in that world, and you miss out on that, and then you retire. I think a lot of guys have that What now? thing. And for me personally, doing nothing was never an option. I would be bored out of my mind. So that’s one thing I always preach to younger guys is find something you think you may want to do before you’re done.

Even in the offseason, you have to work out. So it’s still all based around this one thing. So even your free time is not quite necessarily like, “Okay, all right, go do whatever you want.” And then the season is so structured and you don’t really think about it. Every move is planned. You have your schedule in advance so you know it. It’s not like a surprise, but there’s no free time. I remember when I got traded to the Pistons, somebody asked me: “So, do you just commute? Are you still living in LA?” And I’m like, “No, no. We play every other day. There’s no commute time.”

You definitely have those moments. I kind of made this thing where whenever you get injured—unfortunately I had several times to perfect this—but I would give myself 24 hours to be upset, mad, angry, whatever, feel sorry for yourself. And then after that, you just have to put everything you have into coming back. But there was a specific one. I tore a ligament on the bottom of my foot in the playoffs in 2017. And I remember that season, I had a chef to make sure all my meals were exactly what I needed. I took my pregame naps in a hyperbaric chamber. I would nap in a hyperbaric chamber on off days, ice baths, hot tub, hot, cold, sauna. I was doing everything possible. And I remember the doctor coming in telling me that I tore my tendon, I had to have surgery, and I just broke down. And that was really the first time I really had a break. The other times it’s a shitty feeling, but I broke down, emotionally broke down. I just remember thinking, “Why me?” And I don’t know. I think I just allowed myself to have that moment, and then you have to just flip the switch and go into surgery and go into rehab and go into that whole process of coming back to the court with everything. Everything you would put into preparing for games, you have to put into that. You have to find a way. And for the most part, I feel like coming back from injuries, I did a pretty solid job. It was kind of like the last one. I felt like: I can’t get back to that certain level.

It’s a weird negotiation you’re having with your body like, “Come on, we’ve always done this. Let’s do it.” It actually is funny because you’re like, “Come on, him? He can’t stop you. Let’s go.” And your body’s just like, “Relax. I’ll tell you what we can do.” But I mean, you know it’s coming. Everybody—I mean, LeBron, I don’t even want to talk about, he’s a freak, guy’s a freak—but you know it’s coming and you just have to make that transition as graceful as possible. I feel like as I got older and when I got to that point, it’s like, Okay, you have more time to put more of yourself into your teammates, into making sure everybody else is good. And it sounds like you’re doing this selfless thing, but that’s part of how you contribute and come to terms with it. There’s different ways to be a team player.

I don’t know. It’s hard to answer that question. I think the thing that I am happy with is I know I worked as hard as I possibly could. To use a sports analogy, I left it all out there on the floor. When I was able to walk away, that’s part of the reason—because like I told you, I was doing everything possible. So when you feel like you laid it all out there and you gave it your true best shot, I think it was easier for me to walk away than to be at the end of my career and be like, “Yeah, but what if I had done this or what if I had done that?”

I mean, there’s definitely things where I’m just like, “I wish I had known this or I wish I had known that.” Earlier in my career, I remember Chris Paul always talking to me about screening angles and this and that. He’s talking about the strategy of how he wants to screen, or what I should be doing. It’s not that I was hearing that and being like, “No, no, I know how to do it.” It was like, you couldn’t quite grasp it until you get it. And as an older player, you start to understand these things better and they become second nature. So you’re not having to think through everything. And so now I’ll see an older clip or an older game and I’m like, “My screen should have been…” Stuff like that where it’s like, “Man, I wish I could go back and tell my younger self.” But then it’s also part of that thing where sometimes you have to experience and you have to understand it on your own. You can tell somebody how to do it, but until it clicks, it doesn’t work.

I miss games, especially the end of the fourth quarter of a close game when I’m watching. I’m like, “Oh man, that looks fun.” But then I’ll get a FaceTime from a buddy who’s still playing and he’s in three degree weather in Chicago on Tuesday in January and he’s going to shootaround and you’re like, “Oof, I don’t know if I miss that part.” So there’s the perspective. Like I said, the games were just the best. They’re the best. And then as I got older, some of the things that came along with it, I think that’s what I wasn’t really prepared for. When I wasn’t excited to do that for a full season, I think that’s when I knew it was time to step away.

I had the idea for this show a long time ago. I was watching John Oliver in 2016, and John Oliver’s the way I make sense of real world issues, politics, whatever’s going on. And it also keeps me entertained and locked in with the comedy aspect. And also always watching these reactionary debate shows, morning TV and basketball or sports in general, and realizing that there’s sort of a void in sports entertainment where it feels like you’re learning about some of these bigger issues that affect fans, sports fans, athletes, and even honestly not fans. I think one of my favorite things was talking to somebody this week who was not really a sports fan. They were like, “Hey, that episode is really cool. I didn’t even think about any of that.” We have a research room, we have a writer’s room, and we’re making sure that I’m not just spewing my personal thoughts or feelings about certain topics, but doing the research and saying, “Hey, I played sports and some of this stuff is still confusing to me, so let me do the research. I will present it to you and you can form your own opinion.” I thought there was a void for that.

I mean, there’s tons of podcasts. There’s so many athlete podcasts and they’re great. I am a listener of some, but like I said, I wanted this to be scripted in the way that you can trust that this is researched information and not just me being like, “Today, on The Blake Griffin Podcast, I’m going to talk about sports journalism. You know what? I got a bone to pick with Stephen A. Smith,” and just going at it from just my perspective.

I mean, one of the best parts about making this show is I felt like I got to utilize a research team to learn about all these topics because the idea of the show isn’t like, “Hey, I played sports. I know what I’m talking about.” It’s, “I played sports, I still don’t really know some of these things.” So being able to try to make sense of that from my perspective was the idea. But man, even just taking a step back to look at analytics and it’s like, “All right, when did this start?” And that’s sort of the entry point to that episode is like, “All right, this is how it started. This is what it’s become, and this is what I think is maybe the issue with it, and this is how we can move forward.” We tried to make every episode not just this like, “Hey, here’s an issue, this sucks.”

The “debate over everything” show was definitely something I was aware of. We were sitting in the training room one time and First Take was on, and it was like Stephen A. Smith and Skip screaming at each other, and the topic was our team, and guys are dying laughing because they’re both just dead wrong. It’s not like one guy you’re like, “Oh, he’s got a good point there.” You’re like, “What are they talking about?” And that was the other thing that sparked my idea for the show was there needs to be something where you can feel like you can rely on what’s being said.

I haven’t heard from him. Here’s my pushback on that. I’m hard on specific things that he said. I’m giving you a very real example, something that actually happened and then talking about it—that to me is a little bit different.

That’s a sports media story. So many guys have found out through Twitter what is going to happen to them in their career. I just feel like in this day and age where information is just about getting it out there first, we’ve sort of maybe lost a little bit of decency in how people are being affected by that. And yeah, you can say, These guys get to play sports and they get to make money doing the sport they love. But at the end of the day, I think you should always know first what’s happening in your life rather than everybody else.

Yeah. And I think that the insider can still be a thing. My argument in the sports journalism episode isn’t that like, “Hey, we need to get rid of this.” My argument is that if this is going to exist, we also need to make sure that we keep a space for real journalism.

I just wish that I had known and then there was just an upfront conversation like, “Hey, this is what we’re doing.” I remember after the trade, I remember my agent telling me, he was like, “I got calls from several GMs being like, ‘Why didn’t you tell us we would’ve…’” And it maybe was a situation closer to home. I truly enjoyed my time in Detroit. I really did. So it’s not the fact that I wish I could go back and go somewhere else or do something different. It’s just you just wish that there had been a conversation first.

Abraham Lincoln, obviously. Albert Einstein. Yeah, it was part of the free agency pitch.

I didn’t even process it when I first saw it. We’d had this free agency meeting with the front office and myself, my agent, my brother, and I come downstairs in Staples Center, Staples at the time, and all the staff is around and they all had these shirts on and I’m just saying hi. I mean, it’s people that I’ve known for nine years or eight years at the time. I was just saying hi and I kind of clocked the shirt, but I didn’t start looking at each person being like, “Wait, why did we do this?” I kid you not, said hello to everybody, got in the car, was on the 10 driving home, and the picture of the shirt was everywhere. So it was like 15, 20 minutes later, the shirt was already out there and people were dying. And then I was like, “Oh my gosh, that is nuts.” I didn’t even clock it in real time.

Yeah. And I’ve since talked to Lawrence Frank, and that was even something he expressed to me too, and zero hard feelings.

Yeah, [I] was definitely bummed about that too. I mean, knowing that was his last year and him going back to the Clippers—that’s a thing that a lot of guys do. It’s like, “I want to finish my career in a place that means a lot to me.” That was tough to see.

It’s been great. We have had a lot of conversations recently, and I think we all look back on that time of—Clippers in general, but that time in general also has a spot in our heart. We had a great time. Unfortunately, we didn’t win a championship. But I think we definitely have a sense of pride.

I definitely look back with a sense of pride. I think with the organization, when I got drafted to the Clippers, they were owned by Donald Sterling, who we touched on—historically bad franchise, it was a punchline. And over the course of eight years of being there, we got Chris Paul, we got JJ, we got all these guys, and we were making runs at not only just getting to the playoffs, but certain years I felt like we had a legitimate chance to win a championship. And obviously we ultimately came short, but I look back on it with a sense of pride more than anything, of trying to leave a place better than you found it. And they continued that success even after we left, and it was always a thing where you look back and you’re like, “It’s cool that we were sort of a team that ushered in that era of not being necessarily a punchline.”

I think I had answered a question that was asked of me and I wasn’t like, “It’s crazy they haven’t done…” It was just kind of like, “We haven’t gone back.” But it’s not a thing. I don’t take the stance of we deserve our time or our time to—it’s not really that. Like I said, if we had won a championship and there was never any recognition of that, sure. I mean, maybe you could be hurt about that, but yeah, that wasn’t a statement of like, “I can’t believe they haven’t had it.” That’s not how I feel at all.

No, I’ll carry the flag, man. I’ll carry the flag. I mean, I’ve said it time and again, Clippers fans here are an incredibly loyal bunch. I don’t think anybody can argue that. They’ve been through a lot of ups and downs, and I love it when I’m out in LA and a Clippers fan comes up to me like, “Hey man, I had Lob City tickets” or “I used to watch you play.” It always means something to me. It’s special. So I don’t shy away from being known as a Clippers player at all.

It’s obviously an unfortunate event. I feel bad for the guys that were in the trade coming to the Clippers. Or not necessarily bad, but if you’re a guy who’s 30, 31—Brandon Ingram, for example, he’s 29 and has been to several different places, a great player still, and now you’re coming to a place that doesn’t have draft picks for the next five years. And it’s not to say he can’t go anywhere else after his contract, but it feels like they were penalized and now those guys just kind of had no say and they’re just on that team and they’re like, “But I didn’t do anything.” And then also the fans, just having to sit through the next five years. And it’s not to say they can’t be competitive. I think they will be competitive. They have a great coach and they have solid pieces on their roster, but it’s hard to move forward as a franchise if you’ve been stripped of five picks. As far as: Did the punishment fit the crime? It’s not really even for me to say, to be honest.

Not really. I think teams will introduce a player’s agent to a company, but then the whole thing is—in an endorsement deal, who’s to say what you’re worth, in my opinion? If Aspiration wants to pay Kawhi, whatever it is, that’s on the company. But now if you’re not doing anything for it, huge red flag. I feel like if you had just planted one tree, just one tree—a bush, have a bonsai tree in your house, anything, I feel like that’s where you could just be like, “All right. I guess that’s what they wanted to pay.” So I think that sure, teams do introduce players to brands, but if you’re doing an endorsement deal and you are doing something for it, shooting a commercial, photo shoot, autograph signing, whatever it is, you can’t really argue.

No, I’ve never heard of a player in my time in the league that was just getting paid by this company to not do anything. Never have.

I prefer the basketball, but I think that’s part of it. I mean, there’s always a story. There’s always something going on. And especially now with players being their own brands and having such huge followings on social media, little tiny things can just become their own thing and it’ll grow on its own. I think it’s part of why basketball is so culturally relevant, but I prefer just the basketball part.

It’s funny because earlier you said, “You could have gone the podcast route and you did it the hard way.” And on top of that, I’m like, “Let’s do late night, that thing that’s definitely dying right now.” So, double down on the hardness of it. But I don’t think you’ve seen these shows go away because they’re just a dead format. I think that some of these shows, it’s budget and expense. Like this show, for example, the budget is not huge at all. I mean, I don’t even know what a regular late night budget is, but I would bet a 50th of that. So figuring out ways to do that format, do the late night format, include sports in today’s world. And thankfully YouTube allows people to do that. It’s one of the best things about it, is creators get to just create what they want. If you can figure out a way to take that format, the old school format and make it work in today’s world, today’s budget, I think that’s how you get things to work.

“Is it hard to date?” I’m married now. Not hard at all, actually. It’s been pretty chill.

Well, for one, for budget reasons, for other reasons, we had to block shoot these. So I shot 14 episodes and we had to keep things pretty evergreen and make sure that we weren’t dating ourselves. So eventually I’d love to get that shooting window from shoot to air much closer. I think season two will accomplish that, but eventually I’d love it to be more of a weekly style show where it’s still broader topics, well researched, scripted, but we’re able to have multiple episodes going at one time. And then if we need to activate one, we can and be able to have a much closer to Last Week Tonight, that format. So it’s truly up to date. I really enjoyed doing this. It was so much fun. As hard as it was and as much work as it was, I had a blast. It’s something that I truly, truly enjoyed. So as long as that joy’s there, I’d love to do it till the wheels fall off.

#6726. Past and Prologue: Burberry’s Daniel Lee is Bringing Fashion—and His Extended Family—Home.

Daniel Lee must be considering the notion of home a lot these days. Not just his 17th-century country house in his native Yorkshire, which he bought last year, but his London place, on a leafy 19th-century square, where he has lived for the last five years. Lee, Burberry’s chief creative officer, is enjoying a reprieve from having repair professionals in—the AC has been on the blink, the underfloor heating went awry, and he has already endured one soul-destroying flood. On this hot July morning, he has sequestered himself in the basement, decorated with a beige sectional sofa and a Gary Hume painting, Greenness Is a Kind of Grief. The room looks onto the garden, and Lee has taken to lying out on a lounger; by adjusting its angle and that of the television, he can watch soccer from outside.

“My social life is watching the match on TV; it’s a bit sad, isn’t it?” Lee says in a soft voice accented by dry humor. “I love all sport—Wimbledon’s great—but I prefer the energy of a football match to a tennis match. Tennis is very polite. People lose themselves at football—it’s like a cult, isn’t it?” I didn’t have Lee down as a sports fanatic, but he seems to revere footballers as much as the likes of Skepta and Olivia Colman, whom he loves collaborating with. (Lee supports Arsenal.) There’s also his daily 8 a.m. gym sessions before work. “The bench press is nice, because you can just lie there,” he says, laughing. “I don’t love cardio anymore—it hurts my knees.”

From left: Edie Campbell wears silk poplin trench coat and sequined georgette dress. Alva Claire wears map-print nylon sateen trench coat. Clothes and accessories (throughout), Burberry.

Lee, 40, tells me this as we sit in his garden, the first of our several meetings. In person, Lee is candid, funny, and thoughtful. “Daniel appreciates realness—and openness,” says Skepta. “And he has the best eye. I’d pretty much wear everything he makes.”

Appointed Burberry’s chief creative officer in 2022, Lee has taken the 170-year-old British brand from his highly conceptual debut, all electric-blue blanket checks and graphic red-rose prints, to his more recent collections, widely praised as much for their cool, considered functionality as for the cut and thrust of their forward direction. (Lee has also seen the brand reach pretax profits of over $65 million in 2026, up from an almost $88 million loss last year.) He came to Burberry after three years at Bottega Veneta—an era that flared up like a firework thanks to the success of the Cassette bag and Lido sandals, with Lee quitting before the spark extinguished itself. Before that: six years with Phoebe Philo at Celine, eventually becoming her design director; and before that Donna Karan in New York, following internships at Maison Margiela and Nicolas Ghesquière–era Balenciaga after his graduation from Central Saint Martins.

While the CV reads like a conceptualist designer’s dream, Lee’s Burberry role may be the most reflective of who he really is: pragmatic, unpretentious, driven by a sense of purpose. For his friend Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, who has known him since Bottega Veneta, Lee the person and the designer are one and the same. “The reason I feel so at ease in Daniel’s company is that he is grounded and down-to-earth,” she says. “He has this incredible talent and work ethic, yet there’s no pretense with him, no drama.”

From left: Romeo Beckham wears silk shirt, silk scarf, leather trousers, belt, and biker boots. Simone Ashley wears embellished satin dress, leather shoes, and frame bag. Paapa Essiedu wears nylon sateen trench coat, silk shirt, wool trousers, and leather shoes.

When he started at Burberry, Lee says, “it took me a minute to adjust. What I did in the past was about the dream [of fashion], and it was the accessories that were the focus. The clothes here are still the dream, yet they’re wearable and useful, not just for a show. Designing Burberry makes you question and consider everything.” He sees himself as “a making designer,” he says. “I enjoy being in the moment and working with instinct, with craft, with my hands—the physicality of that.”

Lee’s love of making comes from his family—his father Ian and mother Jenny, his brother Richard and sister Sophie. (Daniel is the eldest.) Ian was a mechanic before he retired, and he now lives in Lee’s Yorkshire home, which is not far from Bradford, where Lee was born and raised. He’s set up a workshop at the back of the house to renovate motorcycles, a lifelong passion, which delights his son to no end—when he and his brother were kids, they would ride the bikes in a field at the back of their house. His mom was the creative one. “She was always making—sewing curtains and baking fancy birthday cakes; she made a Noah’s ark for us, and she even made my aunt, who had a cleaning business, a vacuum cleaner,” Lee says. “It made me think, I just want a job where I can make things.”

Simone wears leather shirt, pleated leather skirt, boots, and bag.

Curtains that Lee’s mom sewed for the family living room now hang in one of the bedrooms at his house in Yorkshire, although “his” is a bit of a misnomer: Lee sees the place as his whole family’s home. The impetus to find somewhere in the area came in the aftermath of his mom’s death just before Christmas 2024. “In those moments,” Lee says, “the creative element of work was soothing—it was like therapy.” He hadn’t even been thinking about getting a place up north, but the undertow of emotion carried him there. His brother and sister-in-law, who live locally, were looking to buy a new home. Lee joined the hunt, and the house he ended up taking was the first and only one he saw. “Before that, I’d always had this quest to live abroad, work abroad, see the world,” he says. “When you’re young, you feel like you’ve got endless time—[then] you realize that, actually, time is finite. My family’s not going to be around forever. I want to spend more time with them.” (One area where Lee would rather keep his private life private is when it comes to dating, though he readily says that he’d like to start his own family: “I would love to have children.”)

His aunt Debbie, his mom’s sister, has moved next door to the 1680s house. It was Debbie who brought Lee to London for the first time when he was 12—they saw the London Eye, took in The Lion King, and ate at the then hip restaurant Sketch. “My aunt was being trendy,” Lee says, laughing affectionately. “She also took me to Harvey Nichols in Leeds. I wasn’t a kid growing up reading Vogue, but looking at the amazing windows at Harvey Nichols and seeing the clothes—that’s when I started to think about fashion.” His grandparents would take him to the Alhambra Theatre in Bradford to see the likes of Chicago (his grandmother’s favorite), which ignited a lifelong love of theater. (On a recent trip to New York, he caught the much-lauded revival of The Rocky Horror Show.)

While Lee’s family has always attended his Burberry runway shows, in the weeks and months after his mom’s death, the closeness deepened. His grandmother came to the show in February 2025 with a photograph of Lee’s mom in her handbag, and it was she who sat with him the night before the presentation as he worked on the last of the fittings. His sister, meanwhile, wore the Bur­berry trench that had been their mom’s. “She wore it to my first show,” Lee recalls.

“One thing about Daniel is that he has never forgotten his roots,” says Lee’s father, “and I think that’s why Yorkshire will always feel like home to him.” That feeling of reconnection is something to which Lee has given a lot of thought. “That’s the real value of the North [for me],” he says. “It gives you a sense of shared ownership of the difficult times, which makes things easier.”

Burberry’s headquarters are on Horseferry Road in London, walking distance from both Buckingham Palace and Tate Britain. Lee’s office and studio are on the seventh floor. He designs Tuesday to Thursday, reserving Monday and Friday for prep days—so the team, he says, can have their weekends free of work. Lee likes to be efficient—the late Virgil Abloh told him that creative directors shouldn’t waste their time emailing, so he doesn’t: He and his team speak constantly via WhatsApp instead.

In one corner of the vast workroom, Burberry archivist Carly Eck has assembled a rail of pieces taken from the 25,000 that the company holds—including the earliest trench, dating from 1917—with an eye to what Lee has responded to: the 1930s Highlander cape, with straps to allow freedom of movement; a motoring overall that Lee riffed on for his fall 2024 collection; and a coat worn by explorer Ernest Shackleton, which Lee also referenced in 2023. Eck and Lee get together at the beginning of every season to help build narratives connecting Burberry past and present. Lee’s intense curiosity has certainly paid unexpected dividends. The ridiculously cute duck hats that he included in his Burberry debut were inspired by drawings in one of the brand’s catalogs circa 1930s, laid out on a table nearby.

“What we do,” Lee says, “is try to provide people with answers about how to live the best possible way. We make clothes to protect people, to make them feel good, ready, sophisticated. I think the fashion is secondary. The design here starts from a place of utility, functionality, practicality—it has to work before it has to be, let’s say, decorative.” His Burberry collections thus far have variously offered blanket-lined parkas, battalion jackets, long kilts, jaunty capelets, and dandyish suiting; what model and equestrian Edie Campbell, who has worked with Burberry since she was 15 (“I still had braces!”), calls “very wearable, but with an edge. It’s joyful, and there’s a lightness and a playfulness to it.” Accessories—the ka-ching! successes for any fashion brand—are on his mind, even if a star hasn’t quite emerged yet.

But if the past is in the room, so is the future. Burberry’s spring 2027 collection, which he showed in September at Chelsea College of Arts—Jodie Turner-Smith, Jonathan Bailey, and Fiona Shaw on the front row; Central Cee on the catwalk—features trenches both diaphanous and etched with embroidery, as well as rendered in leather that’s been lavishly traced with beading; utilitarian cotton drill mixed with sequins; floral blousons and skirts worn with earthy, low-heeled buckled mules; and jewel-like high slingback shoes made a little less precious by being paired with slouchy socks. One thing always on Lee’s mind: making Burberry speak more to women. “The brand is born out of menswear, and the trenches are a very masculine thing,” he says. “We’re always trying to bring more femininity to it.”

Edie wears silk poplin jacket with shearling trim, sequined jersey dress, and leather shoes.

Color is one way into that, and it’s something that Lee has decisively brought to the brand from the very beginning with what he describes as softer, moorland tones; spring 2027, meanwhile, sings with shades of dusky pink, aubergine, duck-egg blue, and a soft-sunny yellow, reflecting the casual, lived-in feel that he wanted to impart on the clothes. Gary Hume, the painter, recalls meeting Lee when they began working on a Burberry project in 2024. Walking around Hume’s studio, they’d touch the art, communing with it. Having now worked with Lee, the artist feels that the designer’s use of color “doesn’t feel like it’s added on—it’s entirely integral to what Daniel does.”

For spring 2027, Lee also worked with the celebrated octogenarian print designer Celia Birtwell, an intrinsic part of the creative explosion in British art and design in the 1960s, along with her husband, designer Ossie Clark, and David Hockney, her close friend. Lee had gone to see the recent Hockney exhibition at the Serpentine Galleries in London—he feels a strong affinity with the Bradford-born artist, who died in June—and a gingham tablecloth that Hockney used as a leitmotif sparked an idea to collaborate with Birtwell, who created a check with a painterly feel to it and some rather charming vintage-wallpaper floral prints. They feel organic and fresh, a million miles away from CAD—or AI. “Celia brings a human hand, an emotional hand, to something,” Lee says, thrilled by what she has done. “We have an incredible archive, but sometimes it’s exciting to see new things.”

From left: Alva wears mohair/silk shawl coat and chevron-knit dress. Romeo wears leather jacket with shearling collar, silk shirt, flocked jeans, and belt.

Lee and I are to meet for the last time at the Regency Café near the Bur­berry headquarters. Founded in 1946, it hasn’t changed much since, still a haven of egg and chips, Formica, and tea so wonderfully strong you could stand a teaspoon up in it. In its own way, the café’s story isn’t so different from Burberry’s: halcyon Britain, yet a Britishness of global fascination. Seated among the Regency regulars are hordes of creatively dressed kids from all around the world Instagramming their full English breakfasts—the very kind of young, style-conscious types who Burberry would want to attract, though not only them, of course. It is an egalitarian brand, as much for the aristo in a beaten-up trench driving a Land Rover as it is for the bloke on the football terraces.

Pride in Britishness is, after all, intrinsic to Burberry. “It stands for heritage and culture, and all the things and all the people that those mean,” says model Alva Claire, and Lee seconds the thought. “We are the most famous British luxury brand,” he says, “but in a way we’re bigger than fashion: We are a British institution. We’re there to celebrate the best of Britain—great creativity and also great locations.” Lee recounts how so many of his Burberry shoots have been deliberately located outside of London—Skye, Somerset, Norfolk, the Lake District—and he readily agrees (while acknowledging the importance of London Fashion Week to Burberry) that it would be great to show somewhere else in the UK. But where? “Chanel did Manchester…,” I say; “Dior did Scotland,” he adds.

Lee on the winding, cobbled streets of Haworth, in West Yorkshire.

Right now, though, Lee is thinking about 170 years’ worth of moments. The anniversary is, he says, “always on our minds. How do we do it justice? We have been ambitious this year.” Indeed: As well as a monthslong campaign photographing 170 people all over the world wearing Burberry, a special exhibition, “The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon,” is at the V&A ahead of the company’s funding of the museum’s new costume wing, opening in 2028; another Burberry exhibition, “Ever Forward: The Archive On Stage,” opens this month in Shanghai.

Anyone would be asking themselves what’s left to do—and for Lee, there’s plenty. Top of mind for him, professionally, is transforming the brand’s retail environments for its 413 outposts around the world. Personally? Well, he wouldn’t mind, at some point in his life, living in a hot country. Yet he’s not in any rush. He wants progress to be measured and meaningful; to take it in stride. “I mean,” he says, smiling, “I really feel quite content.”

In this story: Hair, Mari Ohashi; makeup, Siobhan Furlong; grooming, Quelle Bester; manicurist, Robbie Tomkins; tailor, Della George.

#6725. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6723. Remember When James Bond Was an Adidas Guy?

The search for the next James Bond continues. Over the weekend, Deadline reported that Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult had also screen-tested for the role, in addition to Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O'Connor. But once we've worked out who's getting the tux, there's another question: What sneakers is he going to wear?

As it turns out, their predecessor Daniel Craig got that bit right, too. In 2012's Skyfall, 007 turns up for his MI6 fitness tests in a navy SIS tracksuit and Adidas Gazelle IIs. In the scene, Bond's trying to prove he's fit enough to get back to work, and it's not going particularly well. As a viewer, you'd be forgiven for missing the shoes.

Daniel Craig as James Bond in Skyfall (2012).

But take another look. These were off-the-shelf Gazelles from Adidas's spring 2011 line, the sort that anyone could have picked up the year before the film came out. Bond is a guy whose wardrobe gets examined down to the last cufflink, and there he was in a regular pair of Adidas. His pair came in “dark indigo” suede with “Argentina blue” stripes, white rubber soles, and gold Gazelle lettering along the sides.

(There's a slight difference between the shoes a civilian could buy and the ones in the movie, though. The retail pair had a light blue heel tab, while Bond's appears darker. The fan website Bond Lifestyle suggests the costume department may have changed it, although that hasn't been officially confirmed.)

The Gazelle launched in 1966 as a multipurpose training shoe, and was the German sportswear giant's first-ever sneaker made from suede. The choice to put Bond in the shoe felt notable in more ways than one: In the training scene, the slim sole kept things nice and light underfoot, and the color combo went perfectly with his trackies. But there's also the Gazelle's place in British culture, from the football terraces in the ’80s to the Britpop crowd in the ’90s. So, it makes sense for a Gen-X British spy.

By 2021, Adidas had an official collab to go with No Time to Die. The collection featured all Ultraboost running shoes, with slight nods to Bond's tuxedos and Safin's porcelain mask. The “Q Branch” edition even had a hidden compartment in the lacing cage, handy if your gym shorts don't have pockets.

For a pair that came from a regular ol' Adidas collection, Bond's OG Gazelles are surprisingly difficult to find now. But if you fancy something similar without spending the next six months refreshing eBay, you can start with these.

#6722. Tennessee State Representative-Elect Allie Phillips: ‘Living the Struggle Helps Me Understand the Struggle’

It’s pretty remarkable that Allie Phillips answers her own emails, given the mother of two—and newly elected Democratic member of the Tennessee House of Representatives—has been fielding media inquiries nonstop since last week’s midterm elections. In Nashville the weekend after her win, Phillips’s name was still plastered everywhere—from the Honky Tonk Highway entertainment district to the city’s oldest diner to venerable lesbian karaoke institution the Lipstick Lounge.

In an interview conducted over Zoom a few days later, I spoke to the staunch reproductive-rights advocate and self-described “regular, working-class mom” about turning trauma into action, campaigning while pregnant, and hitting the ground running with a full slate of legislative priorities. Read that conversation below.

Vogue: Congratulations! What did election night look like for you?

Allie Phillips: Election night had a pivot in it. I ended up having to leave the watch party for our county party and move over to another location because it was just so full. When I saw the early vote numbers hit, I was about 20% ahead, and within five minutes, a member of the Republican Party in Montgomery County called me and said, “Congratulations, Representative Phillips.” I was like, “None of the precincts have been reported yet,” and he said, “Your opponent would have to take 75% of the Election Day vote, and that’s just not going to happen, so congratulations.” I was like, “I’m going to wait until the last vote is counted, I don’t want to prematurely celebrate.”

I spent the night with amazing organizations like the Equity Alliance Fund, a Black-founded organization that works on expanding Black political engagement, and TIRRC, the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition. They contributed to so much of my election-night win—they knocked on over 30,000 doors in my district—so being able to celebrate with them was incredible. When we shifted the watch party to a different location, I stood up on a chair in a restaurant in heels, no podium, no microphone, no media, just me and the people that got me over the finish line, and gave my speech that I wrote. It was probably the most down-to-earth, authentic thing that I think could have happened. I wouldn’t change it for the world, because as stressful as it was to have to pivot in the middle of election night, I did what I needed to do as a leader. It was hectic and chaotic, but we got to celebrate together, and that’s what mattered.

Can you talk about the path that brought you to the Tennessee State House last week?

In 2023, I found out that my pregnancy was incompatible at my anatomy scan. I was almost 20 weeks pregnant, and Tennessee had just recently implemented its near-total abortion ban. Due to my daughter’s conditions, my doctor shared that the longer I stayed pregnant, the worse my health would become. I had a daughter at home already, so I didn’t want to put myself at risk. I had to start looking out-of-state for abortion care, and every state surrounding us is also an abortion-ban state, so we had to go even further.

When you have states like Tennessee and others with abortion bans, you have this influx of out-of-state patients bombarding these clinics that are the closest to them, right? So the wait lists were long. The airfare and travel expenses were costly, so I had to start a GoFundMe online because we couldn’t afford the trip to New York City, where we ended up finding a clinic. I went to that clinic 10 days after my high-risk appointment and found out that my daughter had passed in utero, and my body was not expelling her. The doctor said that because the last confirmed fetal heartbeat was almost two weeks ago, I was now at a greater risk of infections or blood clots or going septic, so essentially, we needed to do the procedure now. Within an hour of finding out that my daughter was gone, I was in a gown going into surgery, and I had to do all that alone. My husband wasn't allowed to be there with me. I’d never been in New York City and didn’t know these doctors from Adam, so that experience was very traumatizing.

Phillips testifying about the lack of reproductive freedom in Tennessee during a Senate Budget Committee hearing in 2024.

When I got back home to Clarksville—after the postpartum black hole that I fell into—I was reached out to by the Center for Reproductive Rights, who asked if I’d be interested in joining a lawsuit against the state of Tennessee that was similar to the one in Texas with [Amanda] Zurawski. I don’t think I’ve said yes to anything quicker in my life. I was like, “Somebody has to do something, because this is atrocious and dehumanizing.” The government made me feel like I was gum under their shoe.

I joined the lawsuit, and now I’m the lead plaintiff in the lawsuit. It’s still ongoing three years later. I have not had the opportunity to testify in a trial because the state keeps moving it, but I knew that would take a while. I knew there wasn’t going to be a decision made by the end of the year, so I went and met with my representative at the time, Jeff Burkhart, and shared with him that I wanted help with the Miley’s Law legislation that I wrote that would give exceptions for fatal fetal anomalies. He said he would help me get it up to the General Assembly, but he never did, and then I got sick and tired of waiting around for him to help me and decided that I would just run against him so I could do it myself.

I had no idea what I was doing. I’d never been involved in politics other than voting, and that was, like, presidential elections. I joined my county party and put my hat in for the race, and I ran a 13-month campaign. We raised over half a million dollars, which is unheard of for a Democrat running in deep red Tennessee for a State House office. I had donations from all 50 states. The news coverage of my race was just insane, and unfortunately we still lost, but I took over 45% of the vote. I was pregnant at the end of that campaign. The first three months of my pregnancy were the most grueling three months of the election, August to November.

Being pregnant in August in Tennessee doesn’t sound easy.

Yeah. It was hot and I was super nauseous and I still had to go out and knock on doors. But I did what I needed to do, and then went off to have my son on April 17, 2025, and was still involved. I was pregnant going to marches and stuff, like, you ain’t stopping me. Then I took a little hiatus for that summer. When I came back to work, I started getting more involved again, and then my opponent [Burkhart] died and there was an appointment to his seat, and so I put my name in for the appointment. Our county commission went through five rounds of voting, ended in a tie between me and Michael Lankford, the Republican, and the mayor gave his deciding vote to Michael Lankford, so Michael Lankford was appointed to the seat. He served this last session, so I ran against him this year. We went from being 45% of the vote in 2024 to taking 55% of the vote this year, which was not what we were anticipating. We thought I might win by a couple of hundred votes, maybe, and I think we took it by about 1,600.

I think it says a lot about the dynamic of voters and where they’re sitting with parties right now, because I can tell you, the majority of those voters were not Democrats. There were independents, there were Republicans, and I think that’s incredible. We really had a message of putting working families first; like, I’m a mom of two, I come to work in Nashville every day, my husband works the night shift because we can’t afford childcare, and we do what we have to do to get by. I’m not some wealthy lawyer or entrepreneur with my own business who’s like, Oh, sure, I can be a lawmaker, too. I’m just a regular working-class mom, and I think people want to see more of that in their government. They saw their families in me. They saw themselves in me. I think that’s what made the difference this time versus in the last election, which was just, Oh, she’s all about abortion. What else is she running on? I was like, “A lot of things!” Nobody wanted to talk about them, though, because everybody wants to talk about my story.

Can you tell me a bit about the district you’re now representing?

I am in District 75, which is the western portion of Clarksville. It’s Montgomery County, and the Tennessee portion of the Fort Campbell military base is in my district. Outside of Clarksville’s city limits, we have a lot of really rural farm areas, and that makes this district really unique because we have so much agriculture, and then you come into Clarksville and it’s kind of urban and suburban, a little bit of both. With it being a military town, people are coming and going all the time, so in a small rural district, you might run for office once and then run again and knock the same doors and meet the same people, but in the four years that I’ve lived in Clarksville, I’ve only had one neighbor stay the same. You have people stationed here for a year, 18 months, six months. The doors I knocked in ’24 who supported me, those people aren’t there anymore. It’s different people. A lot of the people that are here don’t vote here, they vote back home or they don’t register to vote at all because they move so much. Clarksville has a university, Austin Peay State University, that’s not in my district; it's in the district next to mine. But there are college students that live in my district, so it’s a double-edged sword. We love the college and we love the military, but it makes it really difficult to navigate the demographic of the voters because they change so often.

What do you think has most prepared you to hold your current office?

I think it’s the experiences that I’ve been through. I grew up in a lower-income family in the small town of Ashland City in Cheatham County. My dad was a construction worker, my mom went to college to become a paralegal, and we didn’t have a lot of money. Growing up, I was taught, You work for the things you want, period. You don’t ask for handouts. Then I went to school to get a bachelor’s degree in multimedia journalism.

Growing up and watching my parents struggle, and then becoming a mother myself and seeing how difficult it is just to be able to afford formula, food, diapers, toys… Everything my daughter had was handed down to us or found on Facebook Marketplace. The older I got, the more I learned that a lot of this is policy. Our General Assembly has refused to cut the grocery tax. We’re one of 13 states that still has one, and it’s at nine and a half percent. We’re paying more for what? People shouldn’t have to struggle to get access to a healthcare professional to get their medication. That’s a policy decision. They could expand Medicaid, but they won’t. Our roads shouldn’t have potholes every quarter-foot or have you sitting in traffic for three hours a day. We could invest in mass transit, but they won’t. I was a single mom for the first three years of my daughter’s life. I was working three jobs while going to college full-time. So knowing and seeing and living the struggle helps me understand the struggle. I’m not a single mom anymore, but we still struggle. If you don’t live this, you don’t understand it. This is nothing against my opponent [Lankford], but we’re both 31 and he’s not married, he doesn’t have any kids, and he lives on property owned by his family.

Completely. He’s a senior banker or something like that, but has he had to serve tables before and rely on tips to pay his bills? He’s never had to worry about getting his children to daycare so he can get to work, and he’s never had to figure out, Well, my kids are sick, so they can’t go to daycare, and now I’ve got to call out of work. My lived experiences are what made me feel qualified for this, because to be a representative is to represent the people, and I grew up seeing what hard work looks like.

What other races were you excited about or watching closely last Tuesday?

The top three races in Tennessee that we were looking to flip were mine, Jesse Huseth down in Memphis, and Brian Goldberg out in Knoxville. I was really curious to know if they were winning voters, and they did. They flipped their seats, and we flipped three additional seats that we weren’t really honed in on. I was disappointed that Jerri Green didn’t win against Marsha Blackburn, but I’m extremely proud of her for how close she got and the campaign that she ran. I was also disappointed in the congressional races that we were looking at with Justin Pearson, Chaz Mulder, and Darden Copeland, but I was very proud of Victoria Broderick for flipping her seat. That’s why you don’t underestimate women; we just show up out of nowhere sometimes! All in all, I’m fairly happy. We have 11 new Democrats going into the House, and I think the chairman said this is the biggest freshman class since either the ’80s or the ’90s. It’s really exciting for Democrats in the state and hopefully gives people more hope that we will continue moving forward.

What’s first on your docket, legislation-wise?

Well, priority number one is my district, always. But as far as legislation, I mentioned Miley’s Law. Outside of reproductive access, I ran my campaign on affordability for working families, so I would love to carry a bill about cutting the tax on diapers and potentially formula. If we can cut the grocery tax, the formula tax goes away, because formula is taxed with our food percentage. I want to cut property taxes for veterans—they served our country, give them a break—and then there was one about creating a lottery for a Tennessee fund for veterans, specifically, that would give them additional help with finding things like healthcare access, mental healthcare, housing, jobs, whatever it may be. My district is so military-heavy that supporting them is so important to me. I plan to be a strong advocate against school vouchers; I am wholeheartedly for fully funding our public schools. I want to make sure our schools are fully funded and that teachers are paid what they’re worth and kids are eating in school, and that we’re not funding private entities with public dollars.

Last question: How are you celebrating your big win and new role?

There really hasn’t been any opportunity to celebrate. I’m still trying to respond to text messages from election night. [Laughs.] I was put on payroll at midnight after the election, so it’s been go-go-go since, but I can tell you that I’m able to sleep better knowing that I’m not stressed out so much by the election. My oldest daughter, who’s nine, was missing me a lot during the campaign, so she's like, “Do you actually get to be home now?” I was like, “Uh, kind of.” She’s my biggest supporter.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

#6721. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6720. The Woven Tote Bag Trend Is Taking Over Runways and Workdays

Woven bags have officially reached icon status.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Is there any other bag that works as hard in real life as the tote bag? When it comes to being on duty and looking good, probably not. The humble tote has come in all iterations: lightweight cotton, supple leather, and suede. But more recently, the runways have been obsessed with making the oversize tote-style bags in luscious jumbo woven iterations. We saw them on the spring/summer 2027 runways at Dries Van Noten, Courrèges, Bottega Veneta, and Altuzarra. And then, labels like Bembien, Naghedi, and Dragon Diffusion are pumping out woven totes like there’s no tomorrow.

A big woven bag offers up texture and interest in a sea of ubiquitous canvas logo totes. It also gives you a bit of resilience so you don’t have to baby your bag on, say, a subway commute or a brisk morning walk where the risk of bumping into others is second nature. It is the working girl’s best friend. That’s just one of the reasons why fashion retailers have fallen head over heels for the style lately.

“Regardless of lifestyle, everyone needs a bag that carries a lot, and potentially the kitchen sink,” Ryan Kleman, Moda Operandi’s VP of buying, accessories, tells ELLE. The great news about a woven bag is that it also seamlessly goes with everything. Tone it down for a day at the office with a button-down top or a casual dress, or take it out for a nice dinner; a silk scarf tied about the strap can be the pop of color or embellishment you might crave for a more formal occasion.

In the case of some of these brands, the woven tote is literal fashion history. Bottega Veneta, for example, first introduced its signature “Intrecciato” woven leather technique in 1975. The fashion house’s spring/summer 2027 collection modernized the technique by applying it to enormous, hulking bags that swayed when worn over the shoulder. Paired with layered sweaters and matching leather belts, the bags felt like a decidedly fresh take on wearable artisanship by creative director Louise Trotter.

In the case of Dries Van Noten, one model carried an absolutely huge woven raffia-effect foldover clutch. Styled with a heather gray hoodie rolled up to reveal leather bubblegum-pink opera gloves with a biker-style cutout and buckle at the hand, the bag itself proved just how versatile a woven piece can be.

If you’re indeed thinking of upgrading your everyday work bag for a woven tote, it’s better to think bigger. “The oversized scale of the bags and the woven construction provide the perfect details to convert a chore into a fashion statement,” says Kleman. “At Moda, we have dubbed this trend the Big A** Bag and our customers are loving it.” This, too, is true: the bigger the weave, the better the carryall.

#6719. 70 Best Gifts for Women in 2026, According to GQ

When it comes to buying gifts for the women in your life, we have one rule: Shop from her wishlist, not her to-do list. Maybe she's got a Sephora's worth of serums in her bathroom, a small fortune invested in vintage Italian glassware, or a closet full of capital-F fashion with “nothing to wear.” Whatever her particular brand of enthusiasm, we've got it well covered, from the latest and greatest beauty to old-fashioned fineries in cashmere and silk. Below, an assortment of some of the best gifts for women at every price point.

Good gifts don't stop here. Explore all our gift guides, then sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more excellent ideas.

British knitwear label &Daughter can count us among its devoted followers, not least for its Sligo V-neck, a Scottish lambswool sweater with a slightly shrunken fit that makes the traditional style feel decidedly of the moment.

Collina Strada made its name from its playful, offbeat designs, and this ring is the easiest way for her to add a little “festive” flair this season without resorting to sequins, though sequins are also welcome.

There's been a lot of commotion around the larger version of Coach's Kisslock bag, but this smaller iteration is every bit as chic. With its structured shape and classic clasp, it's prim and proper in a good way.

This Fair Isle scrunchie from Banana is a cheery finishing touch that makes even the simplest ponytail feel festive. If the wintry knit pattern ain't her thing, there are a few other fun designs to choose from.

We love a precious itsy-bitsy watch, and so does Brynn Wallner, the watch writer behind Dimepiece, who teamed up with Timex to offer up this dainty little number. It's simple, does the job, and makes a lovely gift for someone who feels the same way.

Alexa Chung has a few different irons in the fire these days, but perhaps none hotter than these snakeskin mules with a cute block heel.

A little playful, and straight to the point. Emily Dawn Long's IYKYK wares are modern classics at this point, and an easy gift for those you know who do indeed know.

A rugby for the girls. Boxy and cropped, this one from Buck Mason might finally get her to stop borrowing yours.

Sophie Buhai's signature egg pendant has been around since she first started, and a decade later, I gotta say, it's still a very good egg.

Done up in crocodile-embossed leather, Saint Laurent's giant bowling bag is a canny investment for someone who wants one very good bag to do it all: an everyday carryall during the week, and a posh getaway bag for the next weekender.

A mainstay from New York-based label Silphium, this leather sling bag flaunts a sculptural teardrop shape and an adjustable knotted strap. Each one is made to order, so you better get to it.

No one, at least that I know of, has ever been disappointed by a pair of Comme Si boxers, which can and absolutely should be worn out of the house.

A double-breasted peacoat is good. A double-breasted peacoat cut with these proportions is even better. Ideal for tossing over just about anything.

If she's a self-proclaimed cold girl, Quince's fuzzy merino wool balaclava will keep her noggin (and ears and neck) nice and toasty.

Earlier this year, Acne Studios followed up its much-loved collaboration with perfumer Frédéric Malle with a body wash scented with peach, sandalwood, and musk.

Pepper and rose make a glorious pairing, especially in the hands of Dries Van Noten, who makes some of the best formulations in the business.

Summer Fridays has bundled up a few sunny-day essentials—its lip butter balm, mineral milk sunscreen, and vanilla eau de parfum—in a charming little mini tote perfect for bringing poolside.

We recommended Therabody's Depuffing Wand last year, and we're running it back because it's just so dang good at what it does. Hot and cold treatments in one wonderfully unfussy little device make it a welcome addition to her skincare routine.

Combining gua sha with red-light therapy was only a matter of time. Ora Method's LED gua sha tool also throws gentle vibration into the mix, so she gets a little massaging, depuffing, and skin rejuvenation all in one go.

Between the biting cold outside and the bone-dry heat indoors, winter surely ravages the skin. But a good body oil, like this one from Nécessaire, can help keep her nourished and glowing through it all.

Chanel No. 5 needs no introduction, but I'll give it one anyway. Rose, jasmine, and a little citrus make up this grand dame of fragrances, which smells just as good today as it did a century ago.

If you haven’t heard of La Bonne Brosse, chances are she has. And if one of the French brand’s quaintly demure hairbrushes hasn’t yet found its way onto her vanity, you’d be wise to remedy that.

Over lunch at GQ HQ recently, a few of my colleagues were coming to terms with an inconvenient truth: Rhode's Glazing Milk is actually really good. But good it is: a milky, ceramide-packed essence that leaves skin hydrated, dewy, and looking like the hype machine is onto something.

Eadem's Le Chouchou lip balms have had BeautyTok in a tizzy, and at least a few GQ staffers swear by 'em. This set comes with three versions: Butter Mochi (the no-frills, clear one), Sakura (a milky pink with a sweet tooth), and Fig Sauce (a moody little mauve).

Burberry Goddess is a vanilla perfume for people who think they don't like vanilla perfumes. Warm, creamy, and lifted by a little lavender, it's sweet without smelling like a dessert.

It looks like something out of Ex Machina, and that's just one reason to like Dr. Dennis Gross's LED face mask. The others? Red light to help soften fine lines, blue light to target breakouts, and a purple setting that combines the two.

I won't pretend to know the first thing about hair tools, but the women I consulted for this guide assure me that Shark's FlexStyle is a worthy alternative to the considerably pricier Dyson Airwrap. Defer to their expertise and pocket the difference.

A good hair day is a gift. Kérastase's holiday duo helps make them happen. Inside: the brand's cult-favorite Elixir Ultime hair oil for shine, plus its night serum to work some overnight magic.

The original Glossier You fragrance is a modern classic, and this gift set doubles down on it, with a full-size bottle for her dresser and a travel-size one to take wherever she goes.

A little color for her lips, a little flush for her cheeks, all in one. Pleasing's Big Lip + Cheek is a clever twofer from Harry Styles' beauty brand, which she'll be impressed you know about in the first place.

Look at the lapels on this thing! Hommey's striped robe makes lounging around the house feel like a grand affair, and it comes in all sorts of lively, unexpected colorways.

She can wear these slippers from Mallorca-based Camper while padding around the house, but they'll look just as good out and about. And with a cushy EVA footbed and rubber outsoles, she can be comfortably be out and about for hours.

You can't walk down the street these days without spotting someone clutching an iced matcha, and those daily cafe runs add up. Fellow's beautifully made set, launched last year, can help them save some green while getting their fix.

I'm a coffee drinker through and through, but I'd consider switching allegiances to tea if it meant getting to use this teapot from Balmuda. Just looking at the thing feels therapeutic.

This modish Herman Miller throw features an archival design by Alexander Girard, primary-color enthusiast and founding director of the company's textile division, brought to life by the good folks at Pendleton.

Loewe just added a Pistachio scent to its delicious range of candles. Good luck resisting the urge to light it every night.

No matter how she likes her martinis, they'll always be a little dirty in Maison Balzac's glasses, thanks to the playful glass olives nestled inside. The set comes with two glasses and a matching olive plate.

Rocco's game-changing beverage fridge now has a more affordable sibling. The Essential holds more than 100 cans and costs considerably less than the flagship Super Smart Fridge, while retaining the same compressor.

If status gardenwear is a category she's invested in, there's no bigger flex than a Haws watering can. In cherry red, it feels like a little luxury for reviving your house plants.

With all the high-tech sunrise clocks on the market these days, we've managed to overcomplicate the alarm clock. Maybe some things don't need reinventing. Take this handsome one from Arne Jacobsen, the Danish design legend who also gave us the egg chair.

Fresh on the scene, Typical had the sorta boring idea to rethink the bath towel by adding 2% spandex, making it stretchy enough to move with you and stay securely wrapped. Turns out boring ideas can be pretty great, and these towels are a real treat.

Dorai's sleek stone sink caddy is made from diatomaceous earth, a freakishly absorbent material that wicks away water in seconds, keeping things from sitting in a soggy mess.
