#6718. The Health Benefits of Stair Climbing

We’ve all heard the recommendation to “take the stairs” instead of the escalator or elevator. Not only is it an easy way to squeeze more movement into your day, but research has linked stair climbing to better cardiovascular health and longevity. Even the famously long-lived residents of Barbagia, Sardinia—one of the world’s so-called Blue Zones—spend much of their day navigating steep hills and staircases.

But nutritionist Marián García—better known as Boticaria García, author of Mujeres de Hierro (Iron Women)—takes the humble staircase one step further.

According to Garcia, the benefits of climbing stairs are more numerous than many of us realize: the activity can help increase energy expenditure, improve cardiovascular fitness, strengthen muscles and bones, and even blunt post-meal blood sugar spikes—benefits that become especially valuable after 40, when metabolism, muscle mass, and hormone levels begin to shift.

According to García, consistency matters more than intensity. “When I started running, I incorporated stairs on my way home as the finishing touch to my workout,” she writes in Mujeres de Hierro. “Over time, the habit grew, and today I not only seek out stairs wherever I go—whether at work or in hotels—but sometimes I even climb them carrying grocery bags or suitcases.”

You don’t even need to spend hours on the stair climber at the gym to reap the benefits. García’s recommendation is easy to remember: Simply aim to climb three flights of stairs three times a day. The advice comes from a study in which sedentary adults climbed approximately 60 steps—about three flights—at a brisk pace three times a day, three days a week, for six weeks. By the end of the study, participants had significantly improved their cardiovascular fitness.

García recommends aiming for an effort level of around six or seven out of 10. “You should be breathing harder and your legs should know they’re working,” she says. “You don't need to sprint or arrive at the top completely out of breath—but you shouldn’t be climbing while looking at your phone, either.”

Once stair climbing becomes part of your routine, García suggests making two small adjustments.

Take two steps at a time: “Your stride lengthens, and your glutes and legs have to work harder. That muscle contraction also increases the stimulus on the bone,” she explains.

Vary your pace: Alternate between climbing quickly and more slowly rather than maintaining the same rhythm throughout. “Changing the pace increases the demand and prevents your legs from climbing on autopilot,” she explains.

The strategy is based on what’s known as Frost’s mechanostat—the idea that bone adapts to the loads placed upon it. “If bone receives sufficient and varied stimuli, it understands that it needs to stay strong. If we never challenge it, it becomes complacent,” García says.

One of stair climbing’s most surprising benefits has to do with blood sugar. “Stairs are like a mini gym between floors,” García says. “They engage your glutes and legs, get your heart pumping, break up sedentary time, and increase energy expenditure.”

Research has also found that just one minute of stair climbing after a meal can help reduce the post-meal rise in blood glucose. “No, it doesn’t cancel out the pudding for dessert,” García jokes, “but it gets your muscles to remove some of the glucose circulating in your blood.”

Of course, she isn’t suggesting that stair climbing replaces strength training or cardio. Instead, she sees it as something even more valuable: a tiny habit that’s easy to repeat every day. “It’s a small, repeated action that gradually builds up your health savings,” she notes.

#6717. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6716. Misha & Puff’s First Womenswear Collection Gives Knitwear a New Point of View

The cult-favorite children’s knitwear brand is officially expanding to adults.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Women’s fashion has some of the best designs out there—full stop. That said, every now and then I see a well-dressed kid and think, “Damn, I wish I had something like that.” This is especially true when I see a little one sporting a design from none other than Misha & Puff, a brand known for its ethically crafted, handmade, vintage-inspired children’s clothes. And while my wardrobe carries a playful touch, I’m not necessarily looking for a supersized version of a child’s sweater, but rather the essence of that whimsy. Thankfully, I don’t have to look too far; Misha & Puff just launched its first-ever women’s collection—and it’s more than I could have hoped for.

“Knits are hot. Knits are sexy. The way that they drape, the way that they accentuate your neck, I really do feel like we can do a lot with a knit,” Sophia Roe told ELLE.com over the phone. “For me, I feel really beautiful when I put these clothes on.” The James Beard Award-winning chef—along with her daughter, Mizu—came together with artist Mara Hoffman behind the lens to create a campaign that captures the essence of Misha & Puff, highlighting the craftsmanship and expression of the brand’s new womenswear collection.

“Everything I do with the brand is very authentic and really about what I’m interested in...That’s how the kids’ brand started, with me having my son and then growing up,” Misha & Puff’s founder, Anna Wallack, said on a phone call. “The choice to launch women’s in a bigger way really comes from the pull that I’m feeling as a woman. For me, dressing women and dressing myself is about how we’re working these pieces together. How do I feel in these silhouettes? Who is this character today? I want to keep playing with that in a bigger way.”

Wallack went on to tell me that designing for the collection—which launched today—started with what she described as a “fiber-first” approach. “We work with a Pima cotton in Peru that worked so well for kids because it’s incredibly soft and it’s so wearable, and then to find that I want to wear that all the time for myself; I want to wear our merino wool,” she explained. “Our decision to launch women’s with a bigger collection really was a commitment to doing it instead of just making one sweater here and there.” The result? A range of expressive knits in a color palette reminiscent of the ’70s that encourage the wearer to be who she is as a woman today. With every solid- or heather-hued piece there’s another featuring an eye-catching print or embroidery detail. “I feel a little more permission to explore other ideas in the adult collection and what it means to be a women, too.”

This exploration extends into Misha & Puff’s campaign. Roe shared on a phone call that the idea of partnering with Misha & Puff stemmed from just being a fan of the brand. “I said, ‘I don’t know what we can do but I really want to do something with Anna.’ Little did I know that in the background she was working on this unbelievable adult collection,” she said. Though this isn’t the first project Roe has starred in with her daughter, she explained it was the first where she was shot by another mother, making the experience feel truly special—especially as she comes into her body 15 months postpartum. “I feel kind of hot as a mom. There are a lot of narratives out there about getting back to whatever that pre-baby thing is, and I just kind of rebuke that in every single way. I think what I am now is kind of amazing and I really do feel like Mara was able to bring that out in a way that no one else could have.”

On the vision for the campaign, Hoffman shared that the focus was “seeing how does a woman exist through a space or on the street, and how does she live in it?” Working to capture Roe in a documentarian way, the artist wanted to make sure the imagery felt authentic to both the brand and the people wearing it. “We are lucky to be able to capture little shots of that along the way.” Of course, shooting with a baby can come with its own unpredictability. Luckily, as Roe shared, working with someone like Hoffman helped her relax on set with the reminder, “This is just life.”

#6715. 'Wild Horse Nine' Should Win an Oscar for Its Signet Rings

Wild Horse Nine is a Western. Sort of. Yes, Martin McDonagh’s new film is set on Easter Island (known locally as Rapa Nui) in the Pacific Ocean. And yes, this is the 1970s, with John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell playing CIA operatives who take a break from plotting a coup in Chile to tour the stone moai heads.

But there are also—as the title suggests—a lot of wild horses about, plus a cameo from Tom Waits in a shack in Colorado’s Monument Valley and a hell of a lot of Western accessories. Rockwell’s turquoise belt buckle and cowboy hat almost had me wanting to jump back in time and become a paid-up member of the American deep state. And the big signet rings with chunky stones everyone’s wearing? Look, if you really need me to fictionally assassinate JFK and frame Lee Harvey Oswald for it, I’ll step up.

Costume designer Eimer Ní Mhaoldomhnaigh, who worked with McDonagh on The Banshees of Inisherin, had fun outfitting everyone in colorful shirts and flared trousers. “I really liked the way men dressed in the ’70s,” she says. “There was almost a dandyish quality to them.” But it’s the accessories that really makes the characters. “Anytime you’re doing a fitting [for] a male actor,” she explains, “you’re putting on the shirt and the trousers and they’re like, ‘Mmm, okay.’ Then you put on that belt, you give him a Cuban heel and a cowboy hat and a ring, suddenly they start to stand differently. They get the whole swagger. A costume is never finished until you have all those details.”

This is a film with a lot of those details. Rockwell’s cowboy hat, for example, was custom-made by the London milliner Sophie Lamb, who's worked on films like Phantom Thread. His belt buckle is in the traditional Navajo style of the American West: sterling silver with turquoise inlay, which Mhaoldomhnaigh says she “probably got it on Etsy.” That said, she does a lot of IRL trawling on London’s Portobello Road, too. “I really wanted Sam to wear a chain, but when we put it on with the whole outfit, it felt like overkill—like we were decorating a Christmas tree. You have all those things and then you have to pull back a little bit.”

There’s other great gear in the vein of brash, peacocking men of action. “It’s a very American look,” says Mhaoldomhnaigh. Steve Buscemi, who plays the CIA’s South American boss, is in Coblens glasses with gradated lenses, and a ’70s watch from Rotary. Rockwell has a chunky gold watch from Pierre Jacquard. Malkovich, whose character is still stuck in his ’60s glory days, has this whole pork-pie hat thing happening.

But what really gets me going is the rings. Pretty much everyone—including Waits, who plays Malkovich’s hippie brother—has got these chunky rings on, and of a kind we don’t necessarily associate with gray-suitness of the American establishment today. It’s more dandyish, as Mhaoldomhnaigh puts it: “I was a child in the ’70s,” she says. “I always remember older men wearing those type of rings. My dad had one.”

She was on the lookout for designs which matched her memories, both vintage and new—Malkovich’s ring, which is gold with a black onyx stone, was “actually bought in Liberty,” she says, referring to the famous British department store.

“Martin’s films are always a little bit heightened,” the costume designer says. “That’s part of the fun of it, being able to create these slightly heightened characters.” And dressing up those characters means you can have fun, as McDonagh does, in mocking their big egos. Even so, I’m being deadly serious when I say I’d ransack Mhaoldomhnaigh’s props box any time.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

#6713. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6711. Get Huge’s Director on How Looksmaxxing Is a ‘Trap’ for Men

Chasing physical perfection is a hobby now. This year, the community of men obsessed with climbing the ranks of society via square jawlines and hunter eyes, became a subject of widespread fascination. Once a term known in niche internet forums in the early 2010s, the concept of “looksmaxxing” has gone mainstream. These days, even the casual scrollers among us have probably heard of techniques like bonesmashing and mewing.

But beyond a few self-appointed figureheads of the movement, the question of who is buying into these extreme self-improvement measures has loomed large. In Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death documentarian Stacey Lee gives viewers a deeper look into the lives of some of the looksmaxxing community’s more controversial figures. The three-part Hulu docuseries, out now, follows bodybuilding and biohacking influencer Dr. Tony Huge (whose real name is Anthony Hughes), controversial fitness personality, Connor Murphy, and a handful of other men.

Set largely in Thailand, the series tells the story of how these influencers decamped abroad and continued to post near daily videos of their body modification techniques. Lee also confronts the disturbing pattern of deaths among Huge’s inner circle, some of which have gone unsolved. Ultimately the series raises larger questions about the cultural, gender-driven motivations to push the limits of their bodies. GQ spoke with Lee about her nearly two-year immersion into a small corner of this community, the blurred lines between online persona and reality, and what it all reveals about a generation of young men who are seemingly searching for identity, connection, and purpose through increasingly unhealthy outlets.

These internet influencers create so much content, and there's a performance of masculinity that takes place within it. The topic is incredibly polarizing, but also very nuanced. We wanted to capture this world in a way that was more dimensional than what YouTube feeds allow, puncturing the veneer of performance to show who these people are beyond their online personas. I want audiences to see a more multifaceted view of this world and decide for themselves how they feel about these characters based on what they're seeing.

Looksmaxxing wasn't even a term when we started this project [in 2024]. We initially entered the bodybuilding, biohacking, and masculinity influencer community, which was still very fringe at the time. Tony had started making content nearly a decade ago, using shock value and radical transparency to build his brand. He was willing to do things on camera that others wouldn't, challenging social taboos. Ten years later, we're seeing a new generation of influencers who grew up watching Tony, [biohacking YouTuber Leo and Longevity], and Connor and are now using similar methods. But the algorithm has shifted the goalposts significantly since 2016, pushing the content into a much more extreme and nihilistic space.

I wouldn't necessarily say he was the godfather of looksmaxxing, but he was certainly influential in the biohacking and bodybuilding space. Connor Murphy was probably more directly connected to the origins of looksmaxxing, and Clavicular has referenced him as an inspiration. Tony was part of that same world, but represented a different generation.

Tony was a larger-than-life figure, but it was also a broader cultural moment. Around 2016, we were seeing the first Trump presidency, the post-Me Too movement, and the rise of Red Pill philosophy. There were several figures galvanizing these ideas, and Tony was among them.

I think what you're also referring to is this idea of legacy, right? He created something he believed was his unique gift to the world, but there's a sense that the next generation doesn't recognize him or understand his influence. That disconnect seems to drive some of his pursuit of the next big thing, which, in this instance, is looksmaxxing.

Look, Tony is incredibly charismatic and easygoing. Honestly, filming with him was a really respectful process. I think at times it was really discombobulating because he's always smiling in these videos, and he's presenting as this happy-go-lucky kind of guy, but then you're stopped in your tracks because he's doing and saying things that run against that.

The only other reference I'm thinking of is Andrew Tate, who presents in this very sinister way and has a darkness to him that's front and center. Tony doesn't present that way. For us, it was important to show that and to dimensionalize him. In his eyes, he didn't care if he was a hero or a villain. He just wanted to get his story out there. My approach was that I wanted to humanize him, but it wasn't about excusing what was happening.

It's important in this day and age to approach controversial subjects with an element of humanity while still maintaining journalistic independence. In this world, the boundaries are really slippery because people are performing so much. You really have to have your guard up about what's real and what's not. I don't think it's my job to tell audiences what to think of Tony. It's my job to provide a fuller understanding of who he is and allow them to make up their own minds. Discernment was something that was really important for us to communicate: What you see is not always what you get.

You see it in episodes one and two. [Editor's note: Tony lives with his wife and a group of other women he refers to as his girlfriends.] There's a very specific mentality rooted in Red Pill philosophy, where the role of a man is to control these women and provide for them, but also to assert himself. He's the leader, and they must follow. I think one of the things Tony is always battling is that he presents in such a nice way and isn't aggressive like [his friend and fellow biohacking influencer] Leo was, but there's still this desire to control the women. The women are very strong, opinionated women.

From conversations with Tony during the making of this documentary, I know a lot of the women didn't realize they were coming into a harem. They thought they were his one and only true love, and then they've entered this environment and suddenly they're in competition with one another.

That competition is part of the dynamic of how the harem works. The way Tony puts it is that if they're in competition with one another, they try harder to vie for his attention, love, and affection. That's an incredibly complicated way of pitting women against each other, and somewhat dehumanizing.

What I want to be really careful of is that these aren't a bunch of outrageous, crazy people doing crazy things from the start. It actually begins in a real human place, a place all of us can relate to. I want to be the best version of myself. Yeah, of course I do. That's very relatable.

What happens within this is that some of the needs, in Elon [Muscular, one of Tony Huge’s mentees and a content creator]'s case, a sense of belonging, a father figure, all of those kinds of things that he's craving, aren't solved by taking one pill. These are really deep societal issues that are complex and need to be approached with a multidimensional complexity.

Therein lies a lot of the challenges with this world, because the extreme and the attention keep pushing those goalposts further. You get a bigger jawline, a bigger penis, bigger muscles, and you're still not feeling happy. I think it creates this kind of trap that some men can get stuck within, because the original solution was never going to solve that problem to begin with.

Honestly, it was really important for me to make this. A lot of my prior work has centered on women and diverse perspectives, and it's such an honor and privilege to do that kind of work. But I also recognize I was existing in a bit of an echo chamber, so doing this project took me well outside my comfort zone.

I use this example with kids: When they're scared at night, you shine a light in the room. You look under the bed, you shine a light into it, and it makes the thing that's inside your head less scary. There was a little bit of that in making this documentary, of really looking at it and understanding it, witnessing how people come in, why they stay, and why they also can't leave, and using those things as what I need to teach my son. I need to teach him discernment. I need to teach him the difference between a YouTube influencer who's performing and one who's actually giving genuine, real tips.

In this day and age, where clipping culture and soundbites matter, there's no room for context. We're in a post-truth era, and no one's taking the time to provide context, human dimension, or other perspectives. I want my son to understand how the internet and influencer culture work so he can make his own decisions with more critical thought than what's often taught in the public space.

Yeah, of course. I never wanted to make something that was just another echo chamber. I want this documentary to reach people deep in the heart of the masculinity influencer space. I want them to see it. Everyone's going to have a different reaction, but most importantly, people are talking, and that's what I care about. I need the conversation, the depth of the conversation. That's what this is designed to have.

It's interesting because that question has come up a few times. There does appear to be a turning of the tides. Even within Tony's own universe, his sense of relevancy has shifted. He went from being the most masculine man he could be to wearing eyeliner. It's all become a lot more fluid and therefore a lot more interesting.

I think there's a time we're living through where the power structures that have existed for the last decade are starting to break down. People aren't feeling connected to them anymore, or they certainly aren't serving their needs.

I hope we're at a time of reckoning and change, where people are recognizing that this isn't working. There's so much more awareness about the issues men are facing, and there are specific influencers who are the opposite kind, who are speaking about this stuff more. There are some incredible voices in this space starting to counter the other perspectives out there.

#6710. Ella Emhoff Has Her Curl Routine Down to a Science

Ella Emhoff has long embraced the possibilities of her natural texture. In 2021, the model and knitwear designer showed off her curly helmut of a mullet in the pages of Vogue, declaring her affection for the “almost ugly-chic look.” In the years since, she’s experimented with everything from cropped, curly bobs to voluminous, halo-like shapes. Now, following her latest haircut, she’s got her styling technique down to a science.

Posting to Instagram, Emhoff walks us through her updated curl routine, which incorporates a mix of drugstore staples, cult products, and some clever tools. It’s taken a little trial and error to get here. First up, freshly washed and conditioned hair gets a generous helping of Ouai’s Leave In Conditioner, which she works through with her hands, followed by Kristin Ess volumizing mousse. The latter was something of an emergency purchase, she explains, having run out of her usual Not Your Mother’s Curl Defining Mousse.

The real magic happens with a Bounce Curl brush, which features bristles for smoothing and specially designed edges to separate and shape individual curls. Emhoff sections her hair into two lower layers, leaving the remaining hair around the crown, then brushes and twists each piece outward to encourage definition. Her bangs gets special treatment, with the brush directed forward instead.

Next comes the diffuser. Emhoff uses a Dyson Supersonic Nural hair dryer and employs a fairly athletic drying technique by leaning forward to tackle her bangs, flipping her head around, then leaning back to reach the underneath layers. There’s an awkward in-between phase, naturally. “This is the Weird Al stage,” she announces, her hair reaching increasingly impressive volume.

Emhoff’s most interesting trick comes at the very end. Rather than preserving every perfectly formed ringlet, she breaks the mousse cast by gently pulling down on her curls and running her fingers through them. A wide-tooth comb loosens the ends further, creating a softer, fluffier finish. “I think brushed-out curls are my favorite,” she declares. “I'll say it. Controversial opinion! Or is it?”

The results? A wonderfully buoyant, slightly unruly cloud of curls, with all the character we’ve come to expect from Ella Emhoff’s look. And despite the many steps involved, she’s confident she’s cracked the code. “It's worked every time I’ve done it,” she writes in the caption.

More tips and tricks arise in the comments section, too. “I sleep in a bonnet and use a silk pillowcase,” Emhoff said in one reply. “Usually the two slippery surfaces make the bonnet slipping off pretty unlikely. I don’t care as much about how I sleep in it, as long as they are protected. It’s more about how I care for it in the morning.” She then promised to make a video of her morning routine for a curl refresh—so watch this space. (Feeling brave enough for a curly chop, yourself? Sterling Point hairstylists Chrystal Lotz and DJ Quintero recently shared with Vogue how to exactly achieve Oona’s ’70s-esque curly shag—a perfect cut for fall.)

For anyone whose curls have a mind of their own, this all compounds into a pretty persuasive verdict for your next wash day.

#6709. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6707. What James Gunn’s Firing Means for the Future of DC Studios

For some reason, I foolishly believed they’d get it right this time. James Gunn’s Superman, which formally launched the DC cinematic universe he’s been masterminding alongside Peter Safran, was a refreshing take on a somewhat impenetrable character. I had some reservations about the rest of Gunn’s proposed slate—like following that movie with a Supergirl adventure, which proved to be every bit the misfire I imagined it would be—but bringing a contemporary Clark Kent to the screen was no small accomplishment. Gunn’s tone and his sensibility, I thought, might finally make way for the silver-screen Justice League adventure we deserved.

A silly hope, as proven by Monday’s big news: Gunn and Safran are out, in the wake of the WB-Paramount-Skydance unholy merger. Yet another auteur’s DC regime has been clipped before it could even find its footing. After the shock of the announcement wore off, my mind immediately went to that James Franco meme, the one where he’s about to be hanged. First time?

20 years ago, the idea that superhero C-listers like Iron Man and Thor would be at the top of the film adaptation pyramid while the stars of the Justice League toiled in a constant cycle of developmental destroy-and-rebuild would have been laughable. That’s part of what makes Kevin Feige’s MCU so impressive, of course: not just the scale and scope of his interconnected series of films, but doing it with a bunch of guys who were never all that popular in the larger superhero firmament. But as that regime rose, DC’s fortunes seesawed—with the Christopher Nolan Bat-trilogy as a beautiful outlier—and its fans have had to endure one indignity after another.

Us DC loyalists are basically like fans of the pre-2026 Knicks, or the pre-2004 Red Sox, or the pre-2016 Cavs—take your pick. I wouldn’t even call myself so hardcore, but those were the guys I grew up on, especially as more of a Saturday morning cartoon-watcher than a comics reader. Bruce Timm’s Batman and Superman animated series, the way those two shows dovetailed to make Justice League while also charting bold new territory with Batman Beyond—that was my jam. It was also the era of incredible Fox shows like Spider-Man and X-Men, but never did I think those two would continue to thrive while auteur after auteur tried and failed to do what Timm accomplished before a legion of appreciative 11-year-olds.

It goes back to Wolfgang Peterson’s aborted Batman versus Superman film, a Hollywood sliding doors moment that created the conditions under which a young, hungry Christopher Nolan could prove his blockbuster mettle with Batman Begins and give the greatest hero to ever do it a well-deserved cinematic reset. As Nolan’s stock rose, Bryan Singer’s attempt to restore ‘70s vibes with Superman Returns flopped almost immediately, leaving DC in a Highlander situation yet again. The goodwill Nolan generated with his trilogy gave way to what we came to know as the Snyderverse, starting with Zack Snyder’s Superman reset Man of Steel, a solid film that I could never bring myself to love wholeheartedly.

Historians will tell you it was shareholder thirst to compete with Marvel that spelled doom for Snyder—and the pressure to shoehorn Batman, Wonder Woman and the rest of their squad in to fast-track a Justice League movie. His era certainly cultivated a base of devoted, even rabid stans who will attack anyone who besmirches their leader’s genius. But personally, I spent all of those years in a state of disbelief about the way some of the genre’s sturdiest, best and most crowd-pleasing characters were being subjected to all of this Frank Miller-reject vibes: ultra slo-mo, fight scenes of wanton and artless destruction, not to mention the Gal Gadot line-readings and Bruce Wayne mowing bad guys down in between crossfit sessions. The illest superhero team to do it, in the hands of a guy who saw Jared Leto and thought, “There’s a guy who can succeed Heath Ledger as an Oscar-worthy villain.” Snyder’s step-down from Justice League after a family tragedy and seeing his vision superimposed with Joss Whedon’s was very undignified. But The SnyderCut? Still not for me.

James Gunn’s residency was the most promising thing to happen to the Justice gang in a while, at least for those of us who don’t chug Mountain Dew and listen to Eminem all day. He was the first director in a long time to really, truly understand Superman’s throwback optimistic essence and successfully repackage that for a contemporary audience. Forget about the larger DC universe—what Gunn built in Metropolis alone felt like the beginning of a beautiful universe. Corenswet’s affable take on the character paired with his chemistry with Rachel Brosnahan had me even hoping Gunn would ease up on the big picture and just luxuriate in more Superman adventures. Still, even his slate could only be so fresh: he started in the shadow of Matt Reeves and Robert Pattinson’s The Batman, a critically acclaimed reboot that didn’t square with his vision. At best, we were going to be subjected to the indelicate circumstance of having two different Batmen in production at once. (And that Gunn thought highly enough of Andy Muschietti’s The Flash to tap him for DCU’s Batman film was concerning, for sure.)

But he was building something, and he wasn’t wasting time. Even before he understandably stepped away for a family emergency, Reeves was taking his sweet time to get The Batman II off the ground; Gunn launched his Superman last July and intended to drop a sequel, Man of Tomorrow, next July, one that likely would’ve built up to a Justice League film a little more gracefully than Snyder was allowed to. He may have been indulging side quests a little too freely, green-lighting things like a spin-off series for Skyler Gisondo’s Jimmy Olsen, but his focus on the main play at hand never wavered. The narrative that he was meandering was always in bad faith; look no further than Superman's first act, which breathlessly goes about establishing the status quo of Gunn’s DCU at times to the script’s detriment.

We were already seeing those seeds planted: this past summer’s Lanterns series on HBO, for instance, through which Aaron Pierre managed to turn John Stewart into something closer to a household name hero. (Pierre and Adria Arjona, who is most likely playing Wonder Woman, were set to appear in Man of Tomorrow.) Gunn’s quippy, vibrant vision may not have been for everyone, but he at least deserved the chance to cook a little bit longer. In a weird way, Gunn’s firing feels like one of the first pushbacks to the midterms blue wave. Looking for politics in comic book fare is ultimately asinine, but there’s a reason Superman 2025 was one of the most meme'd movies during the post November 3rd wave of optimism, to say nothing of the movie's plot being a paper-thin allegory for Israel and Palestine.

So what happens now? Who knows. Man of Tomorrow might be released as a sort of post-mortem, or it could be shelved altogether. Does David Corenswet go the way of Brandon Routh? Have we seen the last of this iteration of John Stewart? Will Adria Arjona’s Wonder Woman even get off the ground?

We’re back to square one. Skydance head David Ellision has already replaced Gunn and Safran with ex-MCU producer Jeremy Latcham, a guy who’s more concerned about making movies that’ll play for meemaw, peepaw and the reverend. It appears he'll be a down-the-middle role player who can serve up the most basic, populist take on all of these adaptations. I’m giving up on ever seeing a coherent, let alone genuinely great take on this squad of heroes. Many have tried, all have failed, and the people in charge have only gotten dumber. Go with God, DC faithful. We’ll always have the Bruce Timm cartoons.

#6706. Warby Parker Toasted Its New Intelligent Eyewear Pop-Up with a Book-Filled Celebration

At first glance, classic literature and artificial intelligence might seem like two topics on opposite ends of the spectrum. On Tuesday evening, however, Warby Parker proved they overlap—and share a sense of wonder and discovery. Those tenets are also core to the brand’s new Literatureland pop-up, now open to the public at 666 Broadway in Manhattan’s NoHo neighborhood.

The space serves as an introduction to the new AI-powered Intelligent Eyewear glasses, proudly unveiled by Warby Parker’s co-founders and co-CEOs Neil Blumenthal and Dave Gilboa this week. The innovative eyewear line is made in partnership with Google and Samsung: In each pair, cutting-edge technology allows the glasses to take photos, listen to audiobooks, translate foreign languages, and provide navigation in real time, among many other features.

“We’ve always thought, ‘Is there an evolution of glasses that can help you experience the world even more deeply?’” Blumenthal told Vogue at the celebration. “We’ve just been waiting for technology to emerge—on the hardware side, with the miniaturization of things like batteries and computer chips, and on the software side, with something that provides real utility and can help you navigate the world and answer questions. We’re at that nexus where you can design a beautiful pair of glasses and leverage technology to see beyond what you’d ordinarily be able to see.”

At the immersive pop-up, designed in partnership with creative director Jen Brill, guests perused literary dioramas and set pieces, including supersized books with pictures of the solar system and art by Edgar Degas. Prints of pages from works including Moby-Dick cover the walls, allowing attendees to feel like they are stepping inside an enormous open book. Additional literary references were everywhere you looked—from papier-mâché sculptures nodding to Jules Verne’s Around the World in 80 Days to cakes inspired by Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.

Live music from the Juilliard String Quartet also brought an enchanting air to the party. For an interactive touch, two rooms invited guests to have their star charts read and receive custom poems composed on a vintage typewriter. The latter is where Parker Posey, clad in a deep green gown and brown John Lennon-esque circular Warby Parker shades, mused on the connections between eyewear and the characters she’s played throughout her career. “I wear different kinds of eyewear for movies and parts,” Posey told Vogue. “I wore these pink shades when I played [Irina] Arkadina in The Seagull, and I thought it would be an interesting choice to wear pink lenses for a character who’s an actress. That’s what got me into the colored frames. When you get older, your eyes are tired. Color lifts. You look at yourself, and your eyes aren’t as tired, because they have color on them, which I like.”

The night welcomed attendees from across the worlds of media, fashion, and the arts to check out books and eyewear in a range of formats. Novel-shaped trays held bites like gold-leaf-topped oysters and sunflower tartlets. A gelatin shot bar included a menu written in Italian that partygoers could translate while wearing their lightweight Intelligent Eyewear styles. While wearing the glasses, guests could also learn about New York City landmarks and orientation by viewing a 3D map of the city.

Naturally, given the setting, discussions kept returning to all things literature-related. Posey said that Jessica Craig-Martin’s new memoir I Regret I Am Able to Attend is next on her list. “We’ve got to keep the arts alive,” Posey said passionately. “Lately, I’ve thought a lot about J.D. Salinger and Lillian Hellman, who wrote The Little Foxes. I read everything I could by her about five years ago. There’s also a book called Maybe: A Story, and it’s like a deep breath was taken and the story just came out. My other favorite writer is Elena Ferrante. I’ve read everything she’s written.”

As the glasses become available, Gilboa and Blumenthal hope that curiosity will inspire users to learn something new, too. “Every single person has their own unique and different experience, depending on what they’re asking and what they’re exploring,” said Gilboa. “What gets us most excited is that they enable people to explore the world and can keep their attention in the real world, without staring down at a small device.”

The pop-up is open now, welcoming guests to stop by and experience the invention. “We want to showcase these capabilities in a fun, exploratory space and have people try for themselves,” said Gilboa.

#6705. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6704. Understated, Earthy, and Endlessly Wearable: The Best Olive Green Polishes

The earthy shade adds an edge to fall manicures while still wearing like a neutral.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Like all nail polish colors, green has a vast spectrum, one that runs from electric neon to bold kelly to soft sage and all the way down to deep, moody olive. Of all the greens out there, olive sits in a quieter place. The hue is earthy and a little mysterious, somewhere between a vintage army jacket and an actual juicy olive. It’s a shade we love for fall, since it pairs so seamlessly with black, rich browns, burgundy, red, and, of course, cream.

Once reserved for the brave few, olive has now gone mainstream. Part of the appeal is how wearable it is, offering an unexpected twist without ever feeling too loud. It’s also soft and soothing to the eye, making it an easy shade to wear day after day.

If you’re new to the shade, the easiest way in is to treat it like a neutral. Try it with a camel coat and chunky knits when the weather turns, or a crisp white shirt for something fresh and unexpected. A creamy, opaque finish feels polished and modern, while a glossy jelly or a hint of shimmer adds depth in low light. However you wear it, olive looks effortlessly considered and adds an edge to your style.

Below, we’ve rounded up the best olive green nail polishes to shop now.

A personal favorite, Elia is a muted olive green that looks rich from the very first stroke. The opaque formula glides on evenly in a single swipe and dries to a soft gloss that lasts through daily wear.

Manucurist’s take on olive green feels a touch brighter. It sits beautifully on light and dark skin tones alike and delivers an opaque wash of color. Part of the “Green Flash” collection, it cures under an LED gel lamp and lasts for nearly 21 days.

Essie’s Totally Plaid is an olive green polish with a cream finish that delivers a gel-like shine and depth while still removing as easily as a regular polish. The formula applies smoothly in two coats, giving you rich, opaque color without the need for a UV lamp.

This deep and moody olive green shade is the epitome of effortless chic, pairing easily with everything from neutral knits to bold jewel tones.

Inspired by the lush landscapes of the Mediterranean, this olive green evokes a lighter take on the olive color spectrum. It’s a tad brighter and slightly more yellow-toned, making it a great pick if you want a fresh, sunlit green this fall.

O.P.I’s Suzi is the chic olive green and wardrobe staple of the olive family. It’s a bit darker-toned, radiating earthy warmth and understated elegance. Plus, it’s fast-drying and offers up to seven days of wear.

For those seeking a little more sparkle, this olive green jelly is packed with large green holographic glitters that create a textured finish and catch the light with every movement, adding a spark of joy to your manicure.

Calming and serene, this moss green shade is part of the “Campground Collection”, a four-shade assortment of earthy, comforting colors. Its buttery-smooth application matches the shade’s peaceful look.

This may not look like your average olive green at first glance, but that’s because it has taupe undertones. Once it’s on your nails, you’ll notice the hint of green was there all along. The result is a soft, grounded neutral that pairs effortlessly with cozy fall knits and earthy accessories.

This nail color may be named Pickle, but we see the olive in there. This tangy green with muted yellow undertones feels lively while remaining neutral enough to pair with everything in your wardrobe.

A true olive green, Extra Dirty brings rich, earthy depth to your nails. All you need is one to two coats for a creamy manicure worthy of a fall-season spotlight.

#6703. Denis Villeneuve Talks ‘Dune: Part Three’ and Rebooting James Bond: ‘We Cannot F*ck It Up.’

“I’m out of a job,” Denis Villeneuve said, jokingly. Hours earlier, Villeneuve had signed off on the IMAX 70-milimeter print of Dune: Part Three, officially wrapping post-production on that film—and in turn, a decade-long chapter of the Quebecois writer-director’s working life.

Fresh off this milestone, Villeneuve and GQ had come to the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles for a conversation and a private screening of Dune: Part Two, presented by OMEGA, in honor of his anointment as GQ’s Director of the Year. Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi introduced Villeneuve before the director and GQ’s Zach Baron dove into a conversation that covered his original Dune plans, where Dune: Part Three breaks from its predecessors, and Villeneuve’s feelings about taking over the James Bond franchise.

GQ’s Adam Baidawi and Zach Baron with Denis Villeneuve

“I feel light,” the director of the year told Baron, then added, “Numb.” He was still processing Dune’s end, he said—while also coming to grips with closing the book on “the most rewarding, inspiring, and best ten years of my life as a filmmaker.”

Villeneuve’s first two Dune films have raked in more than a billion dollars at the box office. Part Three appears likely to nearly double that when it hits theaters (and locks up most of the world’s IMAX screens) a week before Christmas. But at one point during his conversation with Baron, the director pushed back gently on the notion of these movies as a “franchise.”

“There was nothing industrial in the way they were made,” Villeneuve said. They were the work of “a bunch of friends”—a familial crew, out in the desert putting things together.

“In French,” the Quebecois director continued, “there is a word—artisanal. They are very personal. Made with a lot of care. They’re little big things—but in a way, they are delicate.”

After all, as sprawling and cosmically grand as they are, these movies are also a deeply personal project for the director, born of images that took root in his head when he first read Frank Herbert’s thick-as-a-brick, notoriously adaptation-resistant 1965 novel Dune at age 13. Later, as Villeneuve racked up credits and clout, people would ask him what his dream project was; the answer was always Dune.

“I kept saying to myself, Someone else will do it one day,” he told Baron. “Another filmmaker will adapt this book again. And I kept waiting, and I kept waiting, until I felt ready to do it myself.”

Herbert wrote five escalatingly bonkers Dune sequels before his death in 1986, but Villeneuve intended to walk away from the table after adapting the first book across two films.

“Trilogies are very dangerous,” he told Baron. “The first movie is a promise, and if you fulfill the promise with the second one, then there’s a feeling of security that comes with that, and you feel that you have a recipe…That’s the trap. Because then you repeat yourself.”

But after wrapping Part Two, Villeneuve found himself unable to stop thinking about Dune Messiah—the second Dune novel, which Herbert supposedly wrote in frustration, believing the audience had missed the point by embracing Paul Atreides as a hero.

Villeneuve said his take on Messiah is “a different beast” than the first two films, built it around the tension between Timothée Chalamet’s Paul and his Fremen consort Chani (Zendaya), who Villeneuve has re-imagined—in a pivotal departure from Herbert’s version—as a nonbeliever who takes a critical view of Paul’s rise to power.

Neel Shah, Timothy Simons, and Michael Lasker

Of course, the specter (S.P.E.C.T.R.E.?) of another franchise hung over the proceedings at the Lucas Museum. Villeneuve, after all, is only technically between jobs; he’s a self-described “monomaniac” who insists that he can only hyper-focus on one project at a time and has been locked in on Dune for a decade, but the as-yet-untitled 26th Bond film is in motion, with Villeneuve signed on to direct.

GQ’s Adam Baidawi, Denis Villeneuve, and OMEGA’s Lucien Jornod

He could say almost nothing in public about the project, or even when he’d begin shooting it—he joked about having “the target of the sniper” on his chest—but spoke of feeling the responsibility not to fail: “We cannot fuck it up. We do not have the choice.”

Over the past week, the casting rumors around Villeneuve’s Bond reboot have reached what our UK colleagues accurately termed the “fever-dream” stage. It might be Callum Turner or Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, but it might be Robert Pattinson, who’s emerged as a surprise front-runner after months of supposition about the part being earmarked for a relative unknown. At some point, toward the end of Tuesday’s conversation, the subject of Bond 26’s lead could no longer be avoided.

“Has the role of James Bond been cast?” Baron asked the director.

“It’s—it’s in the process. In the process,” Villeneuve said with a smile. “I am pushing the gas.”

“Blink once for Robert Pattinson,” Baron suggested, “and twice for Callum Turner.”

Villeneuve, for the record, did not blink. ✦

GQ would like to thank Legendary Entertainment, Warner Bros., and Brianna Smith.

#6701. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6699. Inside the First Competition Between Historic Vintage Timepieces

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

In the automotive world, high-end cars have gone head-to-head since the early 1920s. Judges didn’t evaluate them based on their speed, though—in a Concours d’Élégance, the prize goes to the best-looking vehicles. The tradition continues today in picturesque sites around the world where collectors submit their often very high-end vintage, classic cars. Surprisingly, there has never been an event for vintage timepieces.

Aurel Bacs, the famous auctioneer whose longstanding association with Phillips has shaped the watch collecting world, endeavored to change that. “It began with a meeting where I said, ‘I have a dream,’” he said in a press release. For the very first iteration of this competition, Bacs and Phillips partnered with Swiss heavyweight Vacheron Constantin. They expected to receive maybe 100 to 200 submissions, but the jury was forced to whittle down 550 of them to 34 finalist watches, whose owners were flown out from across the world for the Concours held at the Hôtel Président in Geneva.

“It was the most beautiful evening in the field ever,” Bacs said. At the Hôtel Président, around 200 attendees gathered, along with a jury of 14 watch-industry experts including Bacs himself, Ben Clymer of Hodinkee, writer and historian Nick Foulkes, longtime watch journalist Roberta Naas, and others. Watches could only be submitted for consideration in one category (Chronographs, Métiers d’Art, Chronomètre Royal, Astronomical Complications, Multiple Complications, Design, and Chiming Mechanisms) and were judged based on nine criteria: authenticity, elegance, rarity, impact on the history of Vacheron Constantin and/or on watchmaking in general, provenance, technicality, métiers d’art (artistic crafts), state of preservation, and emotional dimension.

The jurors deliberated over several hours until the winners of the seven categories and a Best of Show were finally selected. Following a cocktail reception, everyone gathered on the lower floor of the Hôtel Président to see the results from the watch world’s first Concours d'Élégance.

The first category featured a smattering of some of the maison’s most important wristwatches, including a highly rare ref. 4072 in stainless steel from 1940. However, it was a yellow gold pocket-watch chronograph from 1929 that won the day. The result was such a surprise that the audience, intimately familiar with the historical importance of pocket watches, audibly gasped inside the room. It made me wonder if these old-fashioned timepieces could regain their lost position as the pinnacle of watch collecting. This piece certainly warranted the love it received: in excellent condition and featuring a white enamel dial with dual registers in an “up-down” configuration, it’s a beautiful timepiece.

This category celebrates handcrafts such as enameling and gem-setting, and it featured a smattering of truly spectacular pieces—mostly sub-40mm wristwatches in precious metals with wild cloisonné or Grand Feu champlevé enamel dials depicting landmasses or animals.

However, a stunning pocket watch set with blue sapphires throughout the bezel and Roman indices won out.

When an older American gentleman stepped on stage to collect his prize, he explained to a stunned crowd that not only had his great-grandfather, Dr. Otto von Frangeš, been given the watch by His Majesty Alexander I of Yugoslavia, its original owner, but that he wore it while sitting in the motorcade during the king’s assassination in France in 1934. Otto’s middle son, Nikola, eventually smuggled the watch out of Yugoslavia by sewing it into the lining of his wife’s jacket as they fled the Iron Curtain in the late 1940s.

In 1907, Vacheron launched the Chronomètre Royal sub-brand, specifically built to endure a life sailing the seas. The model’s parts were anti-magnetic and resisted rusting. The dials were made out of enamel, which could also stand up to the moist atmosphere without rusting. Because they were critical to maritime navigation, timing precision was of the utmost importance, and models from this line frequently won observatory trials (which tested for a watch’s accuracy) that ran from the 1800s to the mid-1900s. Given all that information, the winner is a bit of a shocker: a ref. 2215 from 1976 that exemplifies the qualities of the line but modernizes them in many ways. It doesn’t even feature a full set of numerals, trading them out for a few diamond-set indices. In his acceptance speech, the owner said he wears it on the weekends with jeans.

The Astronomical Complications category is dear to the heart of anyone who appreciates a good moonphase display and also includes timepieces equipped with a triple-calendar, a complete calendar, or a perpetual calendar. Though more modern pieces, such as a skeletonized QP wristwatch from 1987, made it to the final round, it was a wildly neat (and unique) platinum-cased “Cioccolatone” from 1957 that won out. Housed in a 34mm x 43mm rectangular case and equipped with a complete calendar, it’s owned by a dapper Italian collector, who beamed as he collected the prize with his grown son. This would not be this pair’s first time at the podium…

This is a loaded category for Vacheron, which famously makes the most complicated pocket watch and wristwatch in the world, with 57 and 41 complications, respectively. To be eligible in this category, watches were required to have at least two complications—child’s play for VC.

Spanning everything from an enamel-dialed, minute-repeating, split-seconds chronograph pocket watch from 1901 to several Patrimony watches from the 1990s, the winner was the “Don Pancho.” Delivered in 1940, this diminutive yellow-gold timepiece with minute repeater, day, and retrograde date indications was once the world’s most complicated wristwatch. Double-signed by Brooking in Madrid, it sold for roughly $740,000 at auction back in 2019.

A more subjective category, perhaps, than the others, Design included watches “featuring Vacheron Constantin’s signature design, either in the case or through the time display.” One entrant, for example—a wild time-only ref. 4695 dress watch—featured incredibly intricate lugs and a Maltese Cross-type dial. But the winner was nothing short of revelatory. Once again owned by the aforementioned tall Italian gentleman, the possibly unique ref. 6213 is an automatic world timer from 1957 in yellow gold. Based upon Louis Cottier’s famous system, it is so rare that even Clymer admitted he had never heard of it before the competition. The owner’s son described his father returning home with it one day when he was a boy, excited beyond belief that he had finally tracked it down after years of searching.

This category included pocket watches or wristwatches fitted with a minute repeater, quarter repeater, half-quarter repeater, or grand sonnerie—a mechanism that automatically strikes the hours and quarter-hours every 15 minutes. Incredibly, among the entrants was a red gold quarter-repeater pocket watch from the early 1820s with a stunning guilloché dial. However, the winner was another pocket watch dating to 1926 and cased in platinum. Its ultra-thin design, black Breguet numerals, Breguet blued steel handset, and simple silver dial belied the complex mechanism within. The visibly emotional American gentleman who owns it recalled how, as a boy, he would open a chest of drawers, remove his grandfather’s pocket watch, and listen to its minute repeater.

A bonus category, Best of Show went to a truly spectacular wristwatch: a ref. 6448 in platinum with diamond-set indices. Seemingly a simple time-only dress watch, this tremendous piece—which was produced in just three examples in the early 1960s—boasts a hand-wound, 13-ligne minute-repeater movement. Housed in a brushed-finish case with incredible teardrop lugs, it’s the only known example in this metal, and it was notably the last minute-repeating reference produced by the brand for nearly 30 years.

Nominally, the crowd at the awards ceremony was there to judge the merits of a watch, but I left emotionally moved by the stories each watch owner shared about their timepieces. As the very first concours for watches, the format will no doubt be repeated in the future—either by Vacheron, adopted by other brands, or done as a more traditional multi-brand event like the Concours d’Élégance at Pebble Beach.

Acne: It happens to the best of us. And that includes, believe it or not, K-pop megastars. When Yeosang, a member of the Korean boy band Ateez, invited Vogue into his bathroom to spill his Beauty Secrets, breakouts were a major topic.

“It used to be a massive source of stress for me,” the singer confesses. “I would constantly agonize over how I could get rid of all of these breakouts on my face.” That’s where a regimented skin-care routine came in. First, he researched ingredients and products—and luckily for him, he had access to one of the world’s best beauty markets.

His routine includes some products you may recognize (“This [product] helps dissolve dead skin cells and tighten pores,” he says about Stridex pads), along with some new discoveries. By the end of the video, though, you’ll probably have discovered a new product or two, plus a trick for using it.

“Doing this video with Vogue made me realize I use quite a lot of products compared to others,” he jokes. Whatever it is, it’s working for him.

#6697. Zimmermann Hosts a Star-Studded Soirée in Downtown New York City

Katie Holmes, Uma Thurman, and Naomi Watts came out to celebrate the brand’s cruise 2027 collection.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Inside Indochine’s red-lit, retro-inspired French-Vietnamese dining room in New York City, Zimmermann gathered friends of the brand to celebrate its cruise 2027 collection. Presented on the sun-drenched Côte d’Azur in June, the label’s latest served as the perfect bit of vacation and occasion-ready dressing for November in New York. Now that the lineup has officially hit stores, fashion insiders and fans of the brand alike (including Uma Thurman, Eve Hewson, Katie Holmes, and Naomi Watts) showed up dripping in ruffled gowns, sailor-inspired stripes, chunky shearlings, and ethereal lace and silks from the collection. Against the dark, 1940s-inspired tropical salon interior of Indochine, it was the ideal mix of downtown energy and New York glamour.

As champagne flowed through the bar area, glasses clinked while miniature crab cakes and spring rolls were passed. Zimmermann’s sister duo Nicky and Simone Zimmermann could be spotted catching up with friends new and old. “We have a very, very close connection with New York,” Nicky told ELLE in between greeting guests. “It was pretty much when I started the business, one of the first places internationally that I went to in the ’90s, and it blew my mind. It’s been inspirational to us 100 percent.” It was a rare occasion for the brand; for years, Zimmermann has shown at Paris Fashion Week (after presenting in New York in the mid-2010s) and the duo oscillates between Sydney and Paris for most of the year.

Zimmermann’s painterly and intrinsically bohemian flourishes could be seen in the many outfits of guests, all highlighting the vivid cruise collection. Think: decadent silky draped drop-waisted gowns and paneled lace maxi dresses, or, for the more demure, sleek all-black looks that captured the New York essence. “For me, there’s a little bit of a sense of humor behind it—without insulting anybody—it was about the story when Australia actually beat America in the America’s Cup, which is a very famous sailing race,” Nicky told ELLE of the collection’s inspiration.

“I think it was in 1983, and America had not lost the America’s Cup in something like 173 years; it was a ridiculous winning streak, and Australia came along. The inspiration is more about a David and Goliath kind of story,” she continued. “We came along as the Aussies, not established in the sailing world. They were very cheeky, rogue, kind of Aussie young guys up against this amazing, sophisticated establishment of the New York Yacht Club. And they never lost—and we beat them. So in Australia, it’s a legendary story.” Nicky combined the sportiness of sailing gear with the sort of elite New York Yacht Club preppiness, resulting in colorful silk scarf embellishment or sweaters decked out in accessorized pins. “They would hold the most incredible parties and the women were so glamorous and sophisticated and beautiful and not anything that Australia could relate to at the time, so I loved the contrast.”

Conversation was flowing and blooming anthuriums covered the tables as guests took their seats. Nicky kicked off the dinner with a speech, musing on her early days in New York on the Lower East Side and the many parties she attended in Tribeca before sharing more inspiration behind the collection: “It’s about establishment, and then it’s about people, you know, working really hard, coming together as a team, defeating the undefeatable,” she said, with a laugh.

Next came an intimate performance by the singer and Bad Monkey actress Charlotte Lawrence, who sang two of her original songs, then led a folksy sing-along to “Dreams” by Fleetwood Mac. Even the most guarded of celebs and fashion’s elite couldn’t help but bob their heads and sing a tune. As guests dined on a family-style mix of kale salad, spicy shrimp, grilled salmon, barbecued chicken, and steak, the champagne glass clinks slowed as candles slowly flickered and the evening closed out with lemon tarts.

A little yacht-club polish, a little Aussie irreverence: Zimmermann celebrated cruise 2027 in high style.

Socks are one of the more underrated items in everyone's wellness journey. Let's just say this, if you're using terrible hosiery you feet will be begging to slip into these bad boys.

When it comes to running eyewear no one is doing it quite like the folks over at District Vision.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday offer equally good clothing deals. Plan for large retailers and more-established brands to offer deals on Black Friday, and smaller menswear boutiques to hold out for Cyber Monday. As a baseline, expect the better Black Friday sales to start at 20% off and go upwards from there. In the lead up to Black Friday, also be on the lookout for the coveted sale on sale, which has become the norm in recent years.

#6694. Carolyn Murphy, a Lifelong Minimalist, Embraces Maximalism with Her La DoubleJ Collaboration

It’s impossible not to feel a rush of joy the moment you step into an evening hosted by La DoubleJ. And on Tuesday night, that infectious energy permeated a private dining room at the Beverly Hills Hotel, where the Milan-based label threw a dinner party celebrating its new collaboration with supermodel Carolyn Murphy. “It’s relaxing to have fun with your guests—otherwise, it’s no bueno,” the label’s founder, J.J. Martin, told Vogue. “You have to raise the vibration yourself and exude that energy around the room.”

The storied venue was a sentimental location choice for Martin, who grew up in the Pacific Palisades. “My family is from Los Angeles, so this hotel is just like a classic center of gravity for the city, and also a great point between East meets West,” she explained, adding that her grandfather lived in Beverly Hills.

It felt as if the founder had invited a large group of friends—Liv Tyler, Abby Elliott, Jackie Tohn, Sepideh Moafi, and Natasha Rothwell among them—to her splashy, eclectic Milan home. The tables were a feast for the eyes, adorned with multicolored flowers and bright dinnerware, and dressed in a floral tablecloth.

Lela Becker, co-founder and president of Mother, introduced Martin and Murphy at one of Mother’s events around the time of the tragic Los Angeles wildfires, which had destroyed the model’s home. “Lela was like, ‘You’ve got to get out of your hotel,’” Murphy recalled. As it turned out, Martin’s warmth and uplifting spirit were exactly what she needed. “When J.J. and I met at the event, it was like fireworks went off right away.” After the two got to know each other better, Martin floated the idea of a collaboration.

“But I don’t wear prints,” Murphy recalled telling Martin with a laugh. Indeed, the model is a longtime minimalist, but even she couldn’t pass up the opportunity to enter the lively, colorful world of La DoubleJ. “I’m pushing myself out of my comfort zone, and I think that’s why the collaboration was a lovely marriage of our sensibilities,” Murphy explained. Fittingly, she was clad in a champagne-hued two-piece set with bezel-set stones from the collection, which is named Sisterhood of Light.

“My daughter, Dylan, is standing here in the Camelot dress,” Murphy said, pointing out the 25-year-old, who was socializing behind her. Meanwhile, Moafi, who stars in season 2 of The Pitt, was in awe of the collaboration. “It is so diverse and a cross blend of so many different cultures and time periods,” the actor, dressed in a 1970s-inspired patterned blouse and matching trousers, said.

On the outdoor patio, where guests chatted and sipped on cocktails before dinner, Rothwell, known for her role in The White Lotus, looked as though she had just stepped off the set in Thailand, wearing a flowing green-and-teal printed dress. “My stylist Katie Bottomler is the one who introduced me to the brand while I was doing press for The White Lotus,” she shared, with Bottomler standing by her side. Luckily, the label’s airy designs helped Rothwell beat the heat while in Thailand, too. “I’m a plus-size girly, and so I love a brand that considers that and looks good on all body types,” Rothwell added.

After admiring the aforementioned tablescapes and snapping photos, attendees began finding their seats, where copies of Martin’s book Table Energy: Entertaining with Italian Spirit awaited. “By the way, product plug, everything on your table has been made by La DoubleJ,” Martin told the crowd, prompting laughter and applause as they enjoyed artichoke salad, grilled branzino, and filet mignon.
